speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
A resolution was passed by the House of Commons on the 5th May, 1887 to this effect:
That the Customs Department cause to be inserted in the ' Canada Gazette ' at the close of each month a statement of imports, of exports, of immigration and of navigation for the month, and also for the expired portion of the fiscal year.
A search into the records of the Immigration Department show that during 18 years, in which immigration has been under contract of the Department of the Interior, no such return has 'been published, and no such return was ever published notwithstanding the resolution of the House of Commons. And, so far as the department is aware, no such returns were ever published notwithstanding the resolution of the House of Commons.

I wish to call the attention of the Minister of Justice (Sir Allen Aylesworth) to certain articles that have recently appeared in the Montreal papers-the ' Herald/ the * Star,'
' Pa Presse/ the ' Gazette/ the ' Witness/
* La Patrie/ ' Le Canada/ and other daily papers of January 21, 23,	24 and 25
instant, referring to crime rampant in the city of Montreal, occasioned, these papers state, by the readiness with which lethal
weapons, such as stilettos and revolvers, can be procured. Here, for instance, is what the Montreal ' Herald ' published on January 23, last :

Saturday the 'Herald' published, with apt illustration, a story of the 'murder mills' of Montreal-the second-hand stores and pawnshops whose windows are arsenals and over whose counters revolvers, magazine pistols, rifles, daggers, stilettos, deadly weapons of all hinds, can be purchased openly by anybody.
To-day, in grim confirmation of the 'Herald's* plea for some restriction in the sale of the implements of murder, the news is published of one actual murder in the streets of Montreal and two attempts which only missed being murder hy a freak of fate.
In two of the cases the weapons were revolvers in the hands of men who had no good reason to carry arms-men who under sensible and decent legal conditions could not secure arms and would not be allowed to have arms in their possession.
For the murder of Giovanni Oland on Vitre street and for the shooting of Robert Ford on St. Antoine street Saturday night, justice should not be satisfied with the punishment of the assassins alone-it should strike through them at the murderous system that placed this means of murder in their hands and at the law which blinked complacently at the transaction.
Every deadly weapon sold should be sold only under license and only to men. who have secured special permits to carry weapons for good and sufficient reasons. In the absence of such legislation this city maintains itself in the position of a patron of capital crime.
And, Montreal is not alone in this matter, yesterday, walking from these' parliament buildings of 'Canada down Wellington street, as far as the waterworks building. I passed six different second-hand shops on the north side of that street that openly displayed, and offered for sale revolvers, stilettos, daggers and weapons of all kinds. I have here an editorial of the Montreal ' Herald,' of January 23, a part of which I quote as follows :

On Saturday the 'Herald' published an article describing the free and open-handed manner in which deadly weapons are sold in a hundred or more of the stores of Montreal. This morning one man was lying dead and another was in the hospital dangerously wounded as a result of the fact that such weapons can be had for the asking by anybody with a dollar or two in his pocket.
There is absolutely no excuse for the freedom of traffic in deadly weapons which is permitted in this city.
In the same issue of the ' Herald ' there is a cartoon retpresent-ing two foreigners looking at a notice on the wall. The reading is as follows :

Notice.-In order that you may feel thoroughly at home in Montreal the authorities permit the sale to you openly of revolvers, knaves, &c. Thus you are enabled to settle your differences in your native way without the trouble of going to law. If you kill any one it is murder, and if you are caught you will be hung. But it is quite easy not to be caught, so do not let that worry you.

And here, in the ' Herald ' of January 24, is a cartoon entitled ' Accessory Before the Fact/ and representing the city of Montreal as a merchant dealing with a customer, a foreigner. And this is the conversation:
Montreal.-What do you want a revolver for ?
Purchaser.-I want to kill a man who took my girl.
Montreal.-Tut! Tut! Dreadful; don't you know that is very wicked? However, we have them all the way from a dollar and a half up.
Now, Sir, for the last five years I have introduced and urged upon the attention of the government a Bill making it an offence under the criminal law-
I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member (Mr. Lewis), but as he has a Bill dealing with this question already before the House, he cannot discuss the subject at this time.

I bow to your ruling, Sir, and will not discuss the matter further. I ask the Minister of Justice to take over this Bill and make it a government measure. I am perfectly willing to withdraw my Bill if the government will introduce legislation to bring about the result I seek. I think the time has come nvhen action should be taken. And this is not a matter for the city of Montreal, or the province of Quebec, but is solely a matter for the Dominion of Canada.	,

that particular point. subtopic: MR. J. A. MACDONALD AND RECIPROCITY.
MR. J. A. MACDONALD AND RECIPROCITY.
speechtext:
Last week it was my privilege to address an audience in St. Catharines, dealing, among other questions, with reciprocity between Canada and the United States. On that occasion I took the opportunity to state, what I have long believed, that the closer union of Great Britain and her colonies, followed, as I have always claimed, by closer union between Britain and her colonies on one side, and the United States on the other, would be for the benefit and upbuilding of mankind at large. I pointed out that anything that interfered with the drawing closer of Great Britain and her colonies would to that extent militate against the upbuilding of mankind. I pointed out also that a year or two ago, when this last phase of reciprocity between Canada and the United States was proposed,
1 had given considerable attention to investigate the causes at the root of it. We know the old plans: Commercial union, unrestricted reciprocity,- oontinental free trade, annexation to the United States- all names familiar to hon. gentlemen in the House, and the battles royal that were fought up and down the country. We are now all aware that the basis of those movements was wrong. The agitators in those, days appealed to merely sordid motives; cold dollars and cents were held before the people as an enticement to support such a policy. But a new plan was adopted. I pointed out that the plan had taken a different shape. We found that gentlemen were passing up and down the country explaining it from an entirely different view point. We found, as I showed, that the United States discovered a couple of years ago that they were in considerable difficulty from the maximum clauses of their

tariff. We found that the United States press, and politicians on political platforms, were loud in denunciations of the cost of living in the United States. We found further the large centres of population such as Boston, Minneapolis and Chicago, were openly in favour of reciprocity with Canada as the only means of keeping those business centres intact. I pointed out that Canada's vast natural resources also offered a great field for exploitation to American capitalists and business men generally. They had their eye on our resources, and they wanted to get at them. I pointed out that another object was to encourage trade, not along the lines that both governments in Canada had hitherto adopted, that is, lines between the Canadian east and the Canadian west, and between Canada and the mother land, following parallels of latitude rather than meridians of longitude, but that this new movement was designed to encourage trade on lines running north and south rather than east and west. Another aspect of the movement was the advocacy of universal peace especially on the continent of America. I pointed these things out.
I went further, and pointed out that negotiations had been begun by the Rev. Mr. Macdonald, of the Toronto ' Globe.' Whether he was acting as the secret agent of some one else, or on his own personal responsibility, we have no means of knowing. But we do know, and the country knows, that Mr. Macdonald was at Washington, and brought about a condition of affairs, whether as the secret agent of this government or not, has never been officially announced-he brought about the condition of affairs which permits the Minister of Finance and the First Minister to stand on platforms in this country and speak of the ' friendly approaches ' of the United -States to Canada in matters affecting reciprocal trade between the two countries. I pointed out that soon after, if not during these reciprocal negotiations, the Rev. Mr. Macdonald, the editor of the ' Globe,' enlarged his sphere of action and usefulness by becoming the paid agent of Mr. Ginn, a well-known publisher of Boston, a well-known advocate of free trade, and a well-known advocate of peace throughout the length and breadth of the North American continent. Mr. Macdonald, I say, accepted a position in the pay of Mr. Ginn, of the old firm of Ginn, Heath & Company, of Bos. ton. I went further, and I showed that while he had the offer of a salary from Mr. Ginn for his entire services, he had the option of taking a certain sum of money, two or three thousand dollars, for part of his time in the service of Mr. Ginn and he might give the balance of his time in the service of the Toronto ' Globe.' I
stated that Mr. Macdonald had accepted the latter position, and that part of his time was given to Mr. Ginn and to the United States business, that he took his golden dollars from the Boston institution on the one hand, and his Canadian bills from the Toronto ' Globe ' on the other hand for the balance of his services. So that in making his speeches to the country we do not know which paragraph is delivered for the Yankee dollars, and which one for the Canadian bank bills; one cannot well distinguish between them. I think in future this gentleman should label his speeches and say: This paragraph, or this sentence, of my speech, is under the auspices of the Peace Society, and this other one is under the auspices of the reciprocity in trade business. At all events, I pointed all these things out, I pointed out the position which Mr. Macdonald occupied and which he occupies to-day-unless he has abandoned that position. He departed from his biblical training, and attempted to serve two masters. I pointed out further that if I had brought this matter up in the House of Commons, the Toronto ' Globe,' that bedraggled old beldame of journalism, would come out and charge me with hiding myself behind the privileges of parliament; therefore I went out, and upon that platform I made the charge which I repeat here to-day. I went further than that, and added my own conviction, which I repeat here to-day with an extension, and I promise to prove it that the peace agitation carried on by this gentleman was nothing more than reciprocity, continental free trade, commercial union and the annexation of Canada to the United States. That was the ground I took that evening, and before I am through I will prove that that is the platform, or at least the course, taken by these advocates of white-winged peace throughout the country. In days gone by we have often seen the gold bricks of these gentlemen carried around, and therefore when *this new gold brick was presented to us it did not excite us in the least, we knew there was something behind it. Accordingly we carried out an investigation. The public were surprised and shocked, liberal individuals and newspapers were shocked, and the ' Globe ' came out, after having been taunted several days, with a denial which I shall read later on. I may say here that on Tuesday evening, several days after, I was approached by a representative of the Toronto ' Globe,' who furnished the editor with the exact statements which I have given here-I shall come to that in a short time. On Wednesday this prince of ' Holy Willies ' in journalism gave out the following article under this heading:

Under a St. Catharines date line on Monday evening the Toronto ' News ' published the following statement:
Quite a sensation is being caused by a charge which was made by Colonel Sam. Hughes, M.P,. against Editor Macdonald of the ' Globe/ before a Conservative smoker here on Friday evening. Colonel Hughes is credited with making the following statement:- Dr. James A. Macdonald was sent to Washington to open up the question of reciprocity. He is to-day in the pay of Mr. Ginn, a prominent Boston publisher, receiving $2,500 a year to preach reciprocity.
I may point out that what I did say was that Mr. Macdonald was the representative of the Peace Society, but that in my opinion the two things were synonymous, and I will prove it before I am through.
He was offered several thousand a year to give his whole time to this fad of union between Canada and the United States. He was offered $5,000 for his whole time, but preferred to receive part of his pay from the Toronto ' Globe ' and part from a Boston syndicate. Reciprocity means annexation, and annexation the hauling down of the flag which graces these walls.
Now, I will quote from the ' Globe ' editorial:
The Ottawa correspondent of the ' Globe ' was asked to obtain from Colonel Hughes an acknowledgment or a denial of the authenticity of the report in the ' News.'
Colonel Hughes says that what he stated was that Dr. Macdonald, who was a former pupil of his in his school-teacher period, was offered $6,000 per year by Mr. Ginn, the well known ex-publisher of Boston, if he would devote his whole time to the advocacy in the press and on the platform of the cause of universal peace.
I do not know whether the fact about Mr. Macdonald's former relationship is an effort to make it appear that I had violated any confidential information that Mr. Macdonald had furnished to me. I have never learned directly or indirectly from Mr. Macdonald anything about these matters. Anything with reference to Mr. Macdonald other than the mere question of explaining that the word ' reciprocity ' was put in the wrong place, and that the words ' peace association ' should have been used instead, was never broached between the Toronto 'Globe' representative and myself, or put in the report. We did indulge in private conversation afterwards, but I shall not betray the confidence that that gentleman reposed in me concerning the editor of the ' Globe.'
Colonel Hughes drew the inference that the advocacy of universal peace was coupled in Mr. Ginn's offer with the advocacy of peace between the United States and Canada via closer trade relations through the medium of reciprocity, the campaign for which had been first started by Dr. Macdonald when the lat-Mr. HUGHES.
ter was in Washington last spring. Colonel Hughes said that Dr. Macdonald is now receiving $2,500 per year from Mr. Ginn for devoting part of his time to the advocacy of the above causes. Even in its modified form the statement of Colonel Hughes must be classed as a malicious slander.
I stand here to-day and I have the best reason for saying that there is not the slightest deviation from the truth between what I uttered then and what I am saying to-day, that Mr. Macdonald is, or was, unless he has thrown it up, or they have thrown him up, certainly in the pay of the peace society, and certainly drawing gold eagles from that Yankee society, while at the same time drawing Canadian dollars from the ' Globe ' for his services.
Even in its modified form the statement of Colonel Hughes must be classed as a malicious slander.
Well, any one who knows the old hypocrite knows that of all the institutions from time immemorial that has graced or disgraced the public life of Canada the Toronto ' Globe ' is par excellence the superior for its hypocrisy.
The editor of the 'Globe' is at present, as a result of ill health,

I am sorry to hear it-
-travelling in southern California, beyond immediate reach of either wire or letter.
I did not know, until the representative of the ' Globe ' told me that he was down in California. But, when we consider the gold bricks that these gentlemen hand out in that article in order to cover up rascality, the mere fact that this gentleman is in California, where he will be near the Leland Stanford University, the president of which is Dr. Starr Jordan, the great advocate of continental peace with the barriers removed between Canada and the United States, causes us to question very seriously the idea that Dr. Macdonald may not be so seriously ill as he is represented to be. Possibly he is down there recuperating his health, or it might be that having been sent out to preach the peace platform and not being a success, he is remaining there in ordeT that he may receive more lessons in the art from the great master.
As soon as be can be located, Dr. Macdonald will deny over his own name the utterly base inference of Colonel Hughes that he is in any way under agreement with any person to advocate reciprocity with the United States.
Well, we will see about that later on.
The relations of Dr. Macdonald as an advocate of universal peace with Mr. Ginn of Boston have nothing to do with questions of trade of the internal affairs of any nation. It was publicly announced severai months ago in the 'News' as well as in every other

Toronto paper that Dr. Macdonald, while retaining the editorship of the 'Globe/ proposed to relieve himself of much of the detail work of the office that he might devote some part of his time to the advocacy of the cause of universal peace, which he has long had at heart.
So that the ' Globe ' practically admits every word I am saying.
In that work he will be associated with some of the greatest educationists and publicists of America, men of the stamp of President David Starr Jordan of Leland Stanford University

That is the place where every one is supposed to bow the head in solemn reverence.
-and John R. Mott.
Whoever he may be.
It is incredible that men of the type mentioned should receive from the peace foundation of Mr. Ginn any commission to advocate reciprocity or to deal in any way with trade relations.	i
They say it is incredible, but I shall prove it from Dr. Starr Jordan's own speeches delivered in this city, Montreal and Toronto, one of the slickest advocates of reciprocity under the auspicious guise of peace, that I have ever heard. Even the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), in his palmy days, or the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright), cannot -begin to hold a candle to him.
Colonel Hughes' assertion even in its modified form is one that reflects very little credit on the man who made it, and still less on the papers that, knowing the facts, give it currency.	.	. [DOT] 1
And what about the paper that, knowing the facts lies deliberately and maliciously about it ? Never mind the papers that do not know about it, even if they do not tell a straight story, but the paper that knows the whole of the facts, is the one paper that, under the heading of ' A Malicious Slander ' stands out from among the rest and tries to make it appear that I have been telling what is not true. So much for that. It is not necessary that I should go farther than to take from the ' Free Press ' a journal which is particularly friendly to the government and the cause represented by it, published in Ottawa of date December 12, 1910, the following report of Dr. Starr Jordan's speech delivered in this city. He sjooke on the following Monday in Toronto, and I think, he had spoken previously in Montreal:
The movement for peace must have its centre on the American side of the Atlantic ocean. It is recognized also that Canada holds the key to the whole situation.
I remember that the hon. Minister of Marine (Mr. Brodeur), was present and
he straightened himself up and said: What is going to become of the navy ?
Reference was made to the 5,000 miles of boundary between Canada and the United States.
Those of us who were present will remember how beautifully Dr. Starr Jordan treated this matter, and I have to give him credit for being one of the slickest artists I have ever seen on a platform. These are his words:
We are impressed as the people of Europe are, with the fact that along this border there is not a warship

And yet my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster), was just asking for a return about warships a few minutes ago.
-not a soldier, not a gun, nothing

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He had forgotten about Col. Hughes.

I am only quoting this in order that any intelligent man may see the utter fallacy and absurdity of the remarks of this gentleman.
-nothing that looks towards any unfriendly suspicion, so far as violent acts are concerned. The only thing that is wanted to make this boundary ideal is the removal of the customs officers.
Yet the ' Globe ' holds this man up as the prince of peace advocates, and says that there is nothing connecting this man with the advocacy of reciprocal trade relations between Canada and the United States. You should know that Dr. Starr Jordan did not speak of the removal of the customs house officers along the outer border, but only the removal of those officers between Canada and the United States which means that the Yankee flag would fly from the north pole to the sandy plains of Popocatepetl. Then, Dr. Starr Jordan on making that remark-and I remember how beautifully he did it-noticed three gentlemen who applauded him and he said:
I only expected half a group of cheers for that and it is mighty good to get that.
Not content with impressing the business men, -and the rising generation in the city of Ottawa, after showing us the horrors o>f war and the blessings of peace, he insidiously donned the garb of the Meek and Lowly one, and on a Sunday, occupying a pulpit, this advocate of white winged peace could not keep his fingers out of the reciprocity pie. And, here is what we find reported as his sermon on page 2 of the ' Free Press,' column 3, delivered in a Unitarian church in the city of Ottawa by Dr. Starr Jordan :
' The establishment of international peace rested with the United States and Canada/ he said; 'Canada particularly was in a very

unique position because of her relation in politics and common thought to the two greatest nations in the world.'
You will notice that he always slicks us down a little before he ruibs us up. I watched him very carefully, and he is without exception one of the greatest artists I ever saw to captivate an audience ; why, he had the Minister of Marine and Fisheries ready to sell the ' Rainbow ' and the * Nioibe.' Then, after meeting the people in this reverential mood, in a sermon that was well advertised he was catching the spiritual end of the town, he said :
If we can only do away with the custom house officers.
And this in a sermon mark you.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That makes it worse.

He says :
If we could only do away with the customs officers it would be an ideal frontier, said the speaker, in referring to the fact that in 100 years not a gun has been fired between Canada and the United States.
I need not say anything more. I have at least proven to my own satisfaction that the Rev. Dr. Jordan, and the Rev. J. A. Macdonald, and the whole outfit of them were taking Mr. Ginn's money under false pretenses when they would get on a plat form or in a pulpit to preacli the removal of the customs officers between Canada and the United States, for every child in the Dominion knows that means the annexation of Canada, and the dissolution of the British Empire.
