speakeroldname: Hon. WM. PUGSLEY (Minister of Public Works).
speechtext:
This item stood over in order that I might be able to give information to mv hon. friend from St. Anne's (Mr. Doherty) with regard to the new barracks at Longueuil. This, is the information in my possession:
St. Helen's island lias been handed over to the city of Montreal with the exception of three reserves containing the ordnance store buildings and magazines. These are to be reserved for use of the Department of Militia and Defence until buildings are erected for that department to contain the stores, &c., now accommodated there.
Longueuil site was purchased from various individuals in 1846-7 by the Honourable Board of Ordnance for the purpose of a Tete-du-Pont on the east side of Hochelaga bay, below St. Helen's island for the defence of Montreal. It was recently transferred from the Department of the Interior to the Department of Militia and Defence for the purpose of a barrack site.
The area of St. Helen's island is approximately 123 -8 acres and the areas of the three reser-Mr. HUGHES.
various are:-A., 2-735; B., 8-637; C., 9-62 acres.
The Montreal barracks are intended for the accommodation of the permanent troops at the headquarters of the Quebec command, comprising nearly all branches with departmental details and a large number of attached who will be attending for instruction. They will provide a proper school of instruction for the Montreal garrison and the commands and districts. The actual details of the various establishments have not yet been determined, but the totals will probably be about 450 or 500 all ranks, and from 275 to 300 horses.
As regards buildings, there will be approximately 25.
Are these buildings to be used for a military school?
Yes.

Was it considered whether Longueuil was a suitable and convenient place for a military school for the different corns in the Montreal district. It would seem to me that the Longueuil site is a very great distance away from the places of residence of the officers and men, and the headquarters of the different militia corps in the city. If the agreement were that* \\re should have a military school in Montreal it is hardly fulfilling that agreement to establish a military school at Longueuil which I should think must be six or seven miles away, generally speaking, from the residences of the officers and men of the militia -who would use the school
I think there is an electric railway.
You could hardly cross the river on an electric railway.
There is steamboat connection too.

There is an electric railway to the foot of the current and a ferry across the river to Longueuil, but nevertheless Longueuil is a very long distance away from the centre of the city. Taking into consideration the transportation facilities I would be inclined to believe that a school at St. Johns is practically just as accessible as a school at Longueuil would be. When you agree to establish a military school in Montreal and you then establish a military school at Longueuil it seems to me you are far away from tulfill-ing the spirit of that agreement.

Accommodation for 300 horses would be needed and it is very desirable to have a large area of land which could not be got_ right in the city of Montreal. Montreal is growing rapidly and the means of communication with the suburbs are increasing.
Have the militia officers in the Montreal district been consulted about this?

I have no doubt whatever that in accordance with the usual custom the local militia officers have been consulted, but as to that I have no personal knowledge. I do know that the matter has been under serious consideration for a considerable period, and thL is the sober judgment of the Militia Department.

Of course, if the minister is not in a position to tell us positively that the militia officers were consulted it will not help us any for him to make a guess at it. It does seem to me that it would be a highly proper thing that they should have been consulted, and before we can form a judgment on ths vote we ought to be in possession of the opinions expressed by those interested in military affairs in the Montreal district. Until we have that, we are lacking in information essential to enable us to pronounce upon the desirability of locating these new barracks at Longueuil. Of course, so far as I am concerned, I have no idea of objecting to the erection of a military school and to providing the money for it, but we certainly should have some responsible minister here who could furnish us with the information necessary to enable us to form a judgment as to whether Longueuil is the proper place to spend the money for the purpose. It is another instance that impresses the very unfortunate results of the system under which the minister whose department is reallv in question, and who in the last resort decides these matters, is not here to give us the information on which to arrive at a conclusion. We have no information as to whether in the judgment of the persons to meet whose wants the school is being provided this is a suitable place in which to put it.
I thought this was one of the items that was to stand in the absence of the Minister of Militia?
No, it stood in order that I might get some information.

The Minister of Militia should be here to give us the information instead of being down in Nova Scotia running elections. He was not elected for that purpose and is not paid $7,000 a year to do that. It is here he ought to be, and we should not be asked to vote this money without this essential information.

The troops who are to occupy these barracks, are very much dissatisfied with the place. I am told it is very unhealthy, it- is low and at certain seasons, damp, and very inaccessible. There is no reason why it would not be better to have it out at Back Mountain so that the boys from Montreal could attend the military school at night, reaching the place by cars. It is impossible to do this at Longueuil.

(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, I wish to offer a few remarks in reply to what the hon. member for St. Anne's division (Mr. Doherty) has just stated. When the question of building that military school on Lafontaine park came up, I deemed it my duty, in my capacity of representative of that division, to oppose that proposal, as such a building would disfigure that park. Everybody knows that Lafontaine park is the most beautiful park in the city, next to Mount Royal park.
The hon. member for Victoria and Hali-burton (Mr. Hughes) told us that the Longueuil site was unhealthy, but in my opinion the sanitary condition of the place is better than in any other place in the city of Montreal. Moreover, I am informed by the hon. the Minister of Public Works that this Longueuil site was recently given or transferred to the Militia Department. Now, if the government were to buy a site on the island of Montreal, no matter where, they would have to pay for an area 'of about forty acres, from $100,000 to $150,000 in the least, and that site would necessary be at a very great distance away from the centre of the city. I have no hesitation in saying that so far as distance is concerned, the Longueuil location would be nearer and more accessible than any other place available on the island of Montreal.
The island of St. Helene has been sold to the government for $200,000, -as also that portion of land owned by the government on the edge of Lafontaine park.
For my own part I am entirely opposed to that school being built in the vicinity of Lafontaine park.

I should like to ask my hon. friend whether) he considers that there is not to be foun-d on the island of Montreal any land on which these barracks could be built, without disfiguring as he says, or infringing on Lafontaine park.
I think my hon. friend is aware that it would be much more convenient for the young men who shall take the course of that institution to reach those barracks, if they are built on the island of Montreal itself. It is true one may cross- the river at the foot of the current. But the greater number of the interested parties live at too great a distance from the foot of the current where there is a ferry across the river to Longueuil. In the winter time, I suppose they would have to cross over the ice, or pass by the Victoria -bridge, which would oblige them to take a very considerable roundabout way.
I am surprised that my hon. friend, who is one of the representatives of the city of Montreal, should not realize the inconveniences that would result from building

that military school at Longueuil rather than in Montreal, as this means a very considerable difference.

I submit that we have not the requisite information even with the additional light which the hon. member for St. Mary's division is able to throw on the subject. We have the additional information that this establishment is to be used as a military school, but we have no information as to how the conclusion was arrived at that Longueuil was the best place for a military school'. As one who has had some military experience in the past, my strong impression is that you are putting a school in a place which will be highly inconvenient for the service to which it is to be devoted. For a considerable time there has been a very strong desire among those who interest themselves in military matters in Montreal that we should have a school there, and the reason why is that many young men who would be glad to take the course if the school were in the city, find it impossible to get away to St. Johns and follow the course there. You can go to St. Johns from Montreal by rail in three-quarters of an hour and the service is most excellent, so that, so far as convenience is concerned, I would just as soon go from my residence in the city to St. Johns and back as to some point in Longueuil. Nor have we any light as to the particular point in Longueuil at which these barracks are to be built, and the parish is a pretty large one.
Does my hon. friend know where the Tete du Pont is? It is about 190 acres in extent and belongs to the government, and that is the place where it is proposed to build these barracks.

This is the first time I have heard that place mentioned, and I do not know in what part of Longueuil it is. This is a matter of considerable importance, concerning which we ought to have some one here able to tell us all the circumstances and what are the reasons in favour of this location. At first glance it is rather surprising to find that a school which we were to have in the city of Montreal is to be located, instead, at Longueuil, and the only reason given us for that location is that the land can be procured there without being paid for, besides the further reason that if you 'were to build the school in Montreal you would have to disfigure the Lafontaine park. Well, the Island of Montreal is large, and there is a great deal of vacant space in the city on which to build these barracks without at, all infringing on Lafontaine park. I sympathize with the hon. member from St. Mary's (Mr. Martin) in his desire that Lafontaine park, which is very beautiful, should not have Mr. DOHERTY.
any portion of it devoted to this particular purpose, but, after all, we are not reduced to a choice between Lafontaine park and Longueuil. There is a good deal of other space in the city available, and we ought to know whether the men interested, those who are going to use the school, have been consulted. If they have been, we should have the result of that consultation. If they have not, they should be consulted before this matter is finally decided.

What is the use of wasting time? If the minister wants to get his items through, he need not spend any time on this. The Minister of Militia should be here to answer these questions, which cannot be answered without him, and, as far as I am concerned, none of these items should go through until he is present.

There is another point of importance. My hon. friend from St. Anne (Mr. Doherty) has pointed out the drawbacks in having this school outside the city. These are well known to men of the permanent force, but they are in the regular service, and they dare not publicly and openly object, but they do object very seriously, and I can assure the hon. minister that they would much prefer remaining at St. Johns, or Quebec, or the other places where they now are rather than move to Longueuil. The minister might as well hold this item over until the return of the Minister of Militia, and until the officers and men concerned can be consulted. I am satisfied that fifty places can be found on Montreal island a short distance from the centre of the city where this institution could be located with much greater convenience to the men. Many of these men are in business, and the man who wants to retain his position in business cannot give the time required to go from his work and attend this military school if it be at Longueuil, and you might just as well have it at St. Johns as at Longueuil. But if it were situated in the city, or at Back River, or at fifty other places on the island, a business man could attend the course there without trouble, and if night schools were held they would be a tremendous advantage to the city. I would, therefore, ask that this item should stand.

My hon. friend will observe that the item is for Montreal new barracks, and I do not take it that, in passing this item, parliament binds itself to an approval of the Longueuil site. I have said that that is where it is proposed to erect the barracks. But everybody will agree that new barracks are necessary, and that it is absolutely essential in order to carry out the understanding that the $200,000 obtained from the city of Montreal

for the salq of St. Helen's island should be used in the erection of new barracks, that this item should pass. If the Minister of Militia were here I think all he would say would be that because of this Longueuil land being owned by the government, and because of its situation, it was deemed the most desirable place.

Has the minister any report on the sanitary condition of this place ? How high above the river is it and what is the fall ? I am told that it is dead level and that at some seasons of the year it is unfit to be occupied. I am told also that the .ground consists of clay and not sand.
I have great respect for the opinion of the hon. member for St. James, because he lives in Montreal.

I have great respect for St. James, but, as every one knows St. Anne is the particular patron saint of our province, and I am particularly proud to represent a constituency honoured by her name.	t | ;[DOT]

I apologize to my hon. friend. From a military standpoint, I have more than respect for my hon. friend from Victoria and Haliburton )(Mr. Hughes), and my respect grows to admiration of him with regard to military matters. I have great confidence in his judgment and will consider it my business to present to the Minister of Militia the views which he and the hon. member for St. Anne's have expressed. It may be that, instead of using the land which the department owns, it would be better to go to an expenditure of $100,000 or $200,000 or perhaps $400,000 or $500,000.
Certainly, no matter what it is.

In order to get land nearer the city of Montreal, I would say that by passing this vote it is not understood that parliament approves one site or another, but that all it does is approve the erection of a barracks.

If the vote is passed in this way, we shall have voted the money and the barracks will be erected wherever the minister decides without consulting parliament. It is not inconceiveable that parliament might be willing to vote the money for barracks to be erected in a place that would suit the purpose and not in a locality that would not. But to ask us to vote the money and leave the department to decide where it will put the barracks is to give the department absolutely carte blanche. If we are to be judges as to whether this money is to be spent or not, it is an extraordinary position to say that it makes no difference whether the building is to be in one place or another. In other words, that we would be assumed to be as willing to vote the money to put the barracks in an absolutely unsuitable place, if that were shown to be the case, as in a suitable place. I do not wish any misapprehension of what I say. I am not in favour of preventing the construction of the barracks. All I ask is that we should be put in a positon to determine whether the money should be spent wrhere it is proposed to spend it.

May I ask if the hon. member (Mr. Doherty), has received any protest from any military men in Montreal regarding the contemplated site of the new barracks, and if, in speaking as he does, he is expressing the views of these gentlemen ?

I have not received any protest from the military men of Montreal. I have nothing to show me that they know at all that the military school of Montreal is going to he built in Longueuil. This item in the estimates does not convey that information, for it only says ' Montreal-New Barracks.' And, so far as I know, it is only in answer to questions from the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) and myself, put the other evening, that the fact came out that this new building was to be erected at Longueuil. The minister (Mr. Pugsley) is not in a position to tell me that any communication has 'been had with these gentlemen or that they have been consulted in any way. Why does the hon. member for Hochelaga (Mr. Rivet) assume that they know anything about it?
I do not assume it.

Then, how can he expect that they would have communicated with me? And that leads me to say that the main point I would like to bring before the minister is the one I have already mentioned-though he does not seem to pay attention to it-that the absence of consultation with these gentlemen seems to be a reason why this money should not be voted. It seems to me only proper that these gentlemen, who are in the best position to form a judgment as to the location of the military school from the point of view of meeting the needs for which this building is provided, should have been consulted before this vote was proposed. I am not saying that that has not been done, but the minister does not know whether it has been done or not, and neither do I.
I may say, that, on my own responsibility, since I got the information that this building was to be at Longueuil, I have written to some of these gentlemen asking for information as to their views, and I hope to receive that information. The Militia Department may have that information

already, but, if so, surely it should (be at our disposal.

This ought to be satisfactory to my hon. friend, and I hope it will, for the does not want to .prevent the vote from passing, but only wants to (have the local militia officers consulted : I give the assurance to my hon. friend on behalf of the Minister of Militia, and will acquaint him with that assurance, that, if these officers have not been consulted, they shall he consulted with regard to the location of the new barracks. I will also present the views of the hon. member for Victoria and Haliiburton (Mr. Hughes) as to the question which he raised regarding the location. I think he will agree with me that not all the members of the committee, probably not even my hon. friend himself could form a judgment on this question. All he can ask is that before the minister decides upon a location, he should consult the officers to whom reference has been made.

The point is not whether the members of the opposition would toe able to form an opinion as to where this college should ibe located ; the question, as I understand it, is whether the government has come to a decision as to where this building should be erected. If they have, the committee surely is entitled to receive that information. It is not enough for the Minister of Public Works to say : Vote the -money and I will communicate with the Minister of Militia, and then we will do just what we wish. Surely, that is another new doctrine of the Minister of Public Works. He pays -a great deal of respect, to my hon. friend from Victoria and Halliburton-
From the military side.

I listened to his remarks, but it seems to me that if he wished to pay very much respect to my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes) he might accept his suggestion that the item be allowed to stand over until the matter was settled. Surely, after having had so long a time to secure the information -from the Militia Department, and to consider it, he should be in -a position to do something -more than come forward and -say : 'We have not decided.' I would like to know who really did suggest that this building should ibe erected at this point ; was it the Minister of Public Works, the Minister of Militia, or the sitting member for the district?

The deputy Minister of Militia has informed me that it is proposed to erect these barracks at Longueuil, on property owned by the government and, which, of course, will cost the government nothing. It is a large area, something over 190 acres. What I said to my hon.

friend from St. Anne (Mr. Doherty), was that I would represent the views "of the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton who says there is some question about the sanitary conditions there and also the views of the hon. member for St. Anne (Mr. Doherty), that this is not as convenient a place as some others that might be chosen, to the Minister of Militia, and I have given the assurance that, before finally deciding upon the site, which, as at present advised, is Longueuil, the matter will -be looked into further, and the local officers in Montreal consulted. That, I think, is alj that can reasonably be asked.

The promise was merely that the local officers shall be consulted. That having been done, there will be nothing to prevent the department, overriding their views and going on, with the money we have voted, to build the barracks in some place where these officers do not want it. But we would like to know what they think, for this would influence our judgment as to whether the money should be voted to build this barracks on the site proposed. While I do not doubt that these officers will be consulted according to the minister's promise, that does not secure to us the advantage of their opinion, and it does not leave it to us in any way to influence the decision as to whether their opinion should have weight or not. However, I have urged all that I can urge in the matter.

The position of the minister is much the same as that of the farmer who consulted his neighbours about the location for his proposed new bam. He invited them to tea, and afterwards showed them over the place and pointed out localities any one of which might be selected. Then hei said:	' I have
drawn your attention to the facts, and, while I want the benefit of your advice, yet, to economize time I may tell you that I am going to build the barn on that knoll, facing the south.' That is about what would be the result of this proposed consultation. The consultation might not influence the government against putting the building in a place which this House, if it had the information it ought to have, would consider an unsuitable place. But, outside of all that, this House, in my judgment, is doing wrong when we allow estimates to go through in the absence of ministers who ought to be here to give us the information we are entitled to in order to be able to form a reasonable judgment in the question before us. I think the government, when they submit these items, should see that a minister is present who can give the information.

Does the hon. gentleman who is now leading the opposition, and who

has just spoken, take the ground that there will be an objection to any military items going through until the Minister of'Militia returns? If so, we might as well understand it, because I know that they can delay, and even prevent the estimates going through. If the hon. gentleman takes" that view, I will agree to let this and all other militia items stand until the minister returns.

To many of the items there would be no objection. But this is one of so much importance, involving a large expenditure for a public building, that I think the Minister of Militia ought to be here to give us information.

I am not objecting to this item in itself, and I do not care whether the minister is here or not. But I want it understood that the site is regarded by military men-and I have correspondence galore from them about it-as an unsuitable site. In the first place, in order to reach there by land, one has to go across the bridge and then follow the road down the river side. In order to reach it by water, you have to go down below the rapids to cross over. Every one will admit that it is an awkward place to reach, and I am satisfied that every member representing a Montreal constituency will so advise the minister. We can name twenty places on the island more suitable than this is. I am free to say that I believe the reason Longueuil is selected is that the government have, unfortunately, in their possession a little swamp over there, a few hundred acres of land flat, boggy, heavy clay, in the rainy season, practically impassable-I am giving merely the data that I have received. Now the House will freely vote the necessary money for an important institution like this if it is on a proper and convenient site for the officers and men in Montreal to reach. Therefore, in all kindness I ask the minister to postpone the item.
In view of the representations made by my hon. friend I will consent to let the item stand until the Minister of Militia and Defence returns.
With regard to the St. Lambert building the minister promised to furnish us with the options that were procurred in connection with the purchase of the site, the dates and the names.

I have that information.
I find there is only one option on file, that is from Mr. Noel Marcil, dated February 11, 1910, for four months, covering lots Nos. 112, 113, 114, 115 and 116, for $4,140. I have a copy of a resolution of the town council of St. Lambert adopted at a meeting held March 5, 1909, as it is here. I think that must be a mistake, and that it should be 82
1910. There was a letter from the Department of the Secretary of State, dated May 2, 1910, inclosing the resolution purporting to be dated March 5, 1909, therefore, my deputy concludes that there was a clerical error, and that 1910 was the date intended. The site was reported on by Mr. G. S. Gin-gras, clerk of works at Montreal, on the 21st of May, 1910, recommending the purchase.

The hon. gentleman evidently spoke under a misapprehension of the facts when he stated before that there were several options taken. He will recollect what was said bv the representative of the constituency (Mr. Geof-frion).
There was only one written option, apparently. Some times the official of the department visits the different owners and gets their prices, but I would not call that an option.
Were there any other sites in St. Lambert suggested to the government for this building?
That is the only one that was considered by the government, the only one which the town was in favour of. The lot is situated Tight opposite the academy.

The other evening my hon. friend laid on the table some information in respect to a clock furnished his department at Lunenburg. I noticed, in the correspondence of the minister's department, that he asked the clock dealer to write ,the specification himself, and he accepted the price offered under that specification. Is that the policy of the government? I thought it rather strange that the minister should ask a gentleman to supply the clock and at the same time ask him to write the specification.

I do not see why it would not be proper to ask a dealer in a special line of clocks to do so. This was not an ordinary clock; it was a clock to be put in the tower of a building. We asked him to send us a specification of the clock he proposed to furnish, along with the price. We did not accept his price. The chief architect fixed the price that was paid, asking him to take a lower price than the one he had fixed. The chief architect knew from his knowedge, and the information he had got from other clock dealers, what would be a fair and reasonable price, and this gentleman accepted the price offered by the chief architect. Now, with regard^ to asking for specifications, that was done in case of the Quebec bridge; the tenderers were requested to submit their specifications, I mean the proposed new bridge.
Does the minister say that $1,600 is a reasonable price for a clock of this kind?
The chief architect says that it is, according to his judgment.

I would direct attention to the fact that the general price of these clocks supplied in his department heretofore was $700 instead of $1,600. If the gentleman supplying the clock _ was a manufacturer, and this was a special kind, the hon. gentleman's explanation might have some basis. But was it fair that he should have asked tenders from other people supplying clocks, rather than assisting this gentleman to procure the order, and giving him liberty to write the specification himself, finally paying him $1,600 for the clock. Where did this clock come from?

It came from Germany.
Mr. BLAIN1. Why did not my hon. friend purchase it direct from the manufacturer?
What item is the hon. gentleman speaking on now?
I am speaking about some information that was delayed and laid on the table for the information of the House.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The discussion is scarcely relevant to the item in the present resolution.

I would like, by your consent, Mr. Chairman, to give my hon. friend the explanation, so that we may get this disposed of once and for all. There is just as much difference between clocks as there is between watches. If my hon. friend wanted to get a watch would he go around the city and ask people to tender and name the price at which they *were willing to deliver watches to him? There are hundreds of kinds of watches and' hundreds of different prices. There is a great difference between a striking clock and a non-striking clock, which you can get for about $700.
This is a striking clock?

Yes, a striking clock of the very best description, and the chief architect tells me that he got it at the lowest price at which such a clock could be obtained. A small amount was paid to the dealer.	.
What was that amount?
The installing of the clock was included in the $1,600, and there was considerable work about it. It meant repairing the place in the building and all that sort of thing.
My hon. friend cannot have correct information, because there is a payment for making the place and doing what my hon. friend said had been done, to a Mr. Pyke.
That was for arranging the platform upon which the clock stands, putting in the floor and making cuttings in the tower. My hon. friend golf all this information in the Public Accounts Committee.

Here is a clock to be sup-i plied for the Lunenburg public building! Looking over the list of clocks supplied for public buildings in Ontario and other provinces, I find the price to be about $700. I asked why $1,600 was paid for Lunenburg and my hon. friend answered by saying that this is a very rare clock.
Yes, it is a striking clock.

My hon. .friend tells us something, I suppose, that nobody ever knew before, that there are clocks that strike and clocks that do not strike. My hon. friend asks if .1 would go around the city asking for tenders for a watch. I do not know what my hon. friend would do himself but I know what I would do if I were administering a department as my hon. friend is; I would keep the middlemen out.
He was kept out here.

My hon. friend decides how much they will give for the clock. Information is supplied to the chief architect saying that it should cost $1,600. The chief architect and my hon. friend know full well that this clock is not manufactured in Canada. They know where it could be purchased. Why does the hon. gentleman select an individual supporter in Halifax without asking for public competition when he had decided upon the kind of clock that he wanted, and allow this gentleman to supply it? What is a middleman? A middleman is one who stands between the government and the manufacturer, in this case, when, the government want to buy a clock. My hon. friend could have sent for this clock himself, if it was not manufactured in Canada' but instead of that he decides that there- is to be a middleman in it and he selects the one who shall supply the clock. When we are discussing these items the hon. gentleman says that we always have public competition No competition in this at all. What would my hon. friend call this Mr. Shultze who purchased this clock in Germany and supplied it?
I would not call a dealer or merchant a middleman.

I would call a person like this who charges such a price a middleman and a dealer too. The truth is that money could have been saved to the department if my hon. friend had been a good administrator, and if he had not been in the hands of the middleman or the dealer, he can call him whichever he wants. If my hon. friend wanted to carry out the policy in connection with all these important matters of havingpublic competition why did he not ask other people to give prices upon this clock? There were other dealers in Halifax carrying on business in a larger way than this gentleman. This gentleman did not have such a clock in his store. No one else in Halifax had such a clock in his store. Why should my hon. friend select this individual, a political supporter, and say: Put in a clock, and write your own specification when he knew the price at which it could be bought for? My hon. friend comes here and says that there is no middleman in his department. I would like to ask my hon. friend how he draws a distinction between the dealer and the middleman in this case?

As I understand it, a man who deals in any particular article and who buys of the manufacturer gets the article at the wholesale price. I could not go individually and buy direct from the manufacturer, and my hon. friend could not. I do not imagine that the government could, and what I understand is that dealers would get whatever discount there would be from the manufacturer, and that it would be deducted from their price. The wholesale dealer always gets that. Suppose we required to make some arrangements about bath tubs; we would buy them from the man who deals in bath tubs. We would not buy from the manufacturer, and I doubt if the manufacturer would sell to us. In this particular case this gentleman was a dealer in clocks. He would get this clock from the manufacturer at the same price, included in which would be his dealer's reasonable profit, as that at which the government or my hon. friend could get it.
Did the hon. gentleman try to get a price from the manufacturer?
The chief architect says that he knew that was the usual price for a clock of that character.
Did the department obtain a price from the manufacturers?

No. When this gentleman asked a price the chief architect made a counter offer of what he believed the clock was worth. This price of $1,600 includes all the work of installing the clock and the manufacturer would not send a 82J
man from Germany to install it. The chief architect tells me that such a clock as this could not be purchased for a smaller sum. than was paid.

What policy does the department follow in erecting a clock in one public building, and not in another? Does it depend on the wishes of the municipality, or the political influence of the representative of the constituency?

We endeavour to meet the reasonable requests of the different places, and in a new building we sometimes provide for a clock, but if there is already a public clock in the town we do not install one as a rule. My attention has been called to a number of buildings erected 15 or 20 years ago by the Conservative government and they were so scarce of money that they left holes in the towers where clocks ought to be.
They were not so extravagant.
They should not have left the holes there because that was a temptation to the people to ask for clocks.
How would you ever get in if they did not leave holes.
For instance, in the constituency represented by my hon. friend from Huron (Mr. Chisholm) we are putting a clock in the public building at Wing-liam.
Costing $1,600?

The chief architect estimates the total cost at $8,630, and contingencies $1,370, making $10,000. A report from the engineer of the Printing Bureau stated that the boilers had been in continuous use since 1888 and they have been constantly under pressure during all that time. He recommended that these boilers should be renewed, and the chief architect is of opinion that for the safety of property, and perhaps life new boilers should be installed.
Ottawa departmental buildings, fittings, $50,000.
This is a vote which it is found necessary to take practically every year for the purpose of fitting up steel file cases, book shelves, steel drawers, &c.
Is this done by tender after public competition ?

By tenders in each case. There are two companies manufacturing

the steel fittings, the Eclipse Manufacturing Company and the Office Specialty Company.
Ottawa departmental buildings, improvements in lavatories, plumbing, &o., $10,000.
I would again point out that the sanitary accommodation in this building is in a prehistoric condition, some of the accommodation is not up to the standard of a modern railway closet.
I remember a conversation with my hon. friend and I gave direction to the chief architect to have the improvements made. He reported to me that he had them made as far as the premises would permit.
Nothing was done at all.
I regret that it was not possible to make the improvements as complete as they should be made.
Nothing was done at all.
I shall have to ask the chief architect to see my hon. friend because he says that considerable work was done.
I do not think that even a drop of paint was put on the. bathrooms and barber shop.
A shower bath was put in.

I have not seen it. The bathroom should be taken out of the barber shop as any one coming from a bathroom is liable to strike the arm of the barber while he is shaving a customer.
Another matter of importance is that the water of Ottawa is certainly impregnated with typhoid. I believe there are a couple of places in the building where we can get water which is supposed to be purified. If it is a good system, why not put it through all the different departmental buildings ?
I made a statement last night of what has been done. We have one supply of purified water on each floor.
Why not have it all over the offices ?
We are providing for that. We have communicated with the Finance Department with a view of putting that system in each of the blocks.

It seems to me there is an obligation resting on others' as well as on the government. We pay a consideration to the city of Ottawa for the provision they have made to give us water for these buildings. It is natural to assume that that means healthy and pure water, and if nothing is dished up but what is mixed Mr. PUGSLEY.
with sewage we are throwing away our money and are very careless with regard to the health of those who come from every part of the country to spend four to six months of the year attending parliament. 1 thought that the First Minister the other evening spoke about this in a very trifling and flippant manner. It is too serious to be dealt with in this way. There is an obligation on the city to furnish pure water in proper quantity and if they do not do that, we should revise our contract with them. There is an obligation resting on the health officer to see that the health of the people is properly loked after in regard to the water supplied for drinking, It was said as an excuse for the failure to analyse the water from month to month, that the health officer had not bottles to send it in. What a trivial excuse, what supreme carelessness it is. What is the city council doing ? What kind of a health officer have we ? Are these conditions to be allowed to continue with the imminent danger which exists ? Already immense trouble, expense, suffering and death have been brought to many people in this city on account of the impure water they are obliged to use. This condition of things has been going on for weeks and it is time the department should wake up and realize the importance of forcing the city to take prompt action. If the city have not an efficient health officer they should call on him to resign and put some competent man in his place, and not allow the health of the people to suffer through so apparent a dereliction of duty in the management of the health department.

When the officers of the council have been going around indulging in pyrotechnical displays and using their energies in kow-towing to the powers that be, you cannot expect them to attend to the business of the city, and I am astonished that my hon. friend from Grey (Mr. Sproule) should expect anything of the kind. The attention of the city council has been drawn for years to the danger. A certain medical officer has frequently pointed out to the council and to the health officer the fact that this city is at the mercy of the towns along the river and that steps should be taken to provide a remedy. It would be well to follow the suggestion of the hon. member for Grey and stir the city council up.
We do not appoint the health officer. He is appointed by the Ontario government.
No, by the city council.

At all events we have no control over him. My hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) is so accustomed to fault finding that he naturally pitches

right in to the city council and its health officer, hut we ought to have some little consideration for them. I believe they are doing the best they can in the serious conditions with which they are confronted. Either some other source must be obtained from which the supply of water can be got or else something should be done to sterilize and purify the water contaminated by the sewage which is emptied into the Ottawa river from towns such as Aylmer, Arnprior, Pembroke and Renfrew and others along its banks. The city of Ottawa is doing the best it can. It has engineers endeavouring to find some other source (from which water can be obtained. The only thing we can do, in the discharge of our duty, is to sterilize the water and make it as palatable as we can. Our officials are giving their utmost attention to that; and if hon. members will be careful to drink only the sterilized water, they need not fear any danger.
The hon. minister says that I am so accustomed to fault finding that I cannot allow an opportunity like this to pass.
Hear, hear.
Does he say that there is not just ground for fault finding?
Not against the health officer.	.

Parliament is asked to vote a large sum to the city of Ottawa for the supply of water, and we must presume that the citv is bound to supply pure and healthy water. If water of that kind is not supplied we ought to stop the pay. The only parties which parliament can hold responsible are the ministers of the Crown. All the minister can say is that he supposes the health officer is doing what he should, but I remember distinctly that instructions were given the health officer to have the water analysed every week or every month but, in reply to a question as to when the last analysis was made, we are told that it was made away back in the month of November. Then the question was asked why did the health officer not attend to this, and the reply was that the city council would see that this was done. When the health officer was asked why he had not had an analysis made, his excuse was that he had not proper bottles in which to send the water to be analysed. Such an excuse should not be tolerated. It is true we can get our water sterilized by distillation, but it may be found that in our private rooms and in places where we take our meals, no such water is provided.
Why should not private individuals boil the water and so sterilize it just as is being done here?

Why should not private individuals look to the health officer whose duty it is to see that we are furnished with pure water? Why should they be obliged to drink sewage water because of the dilatoriness of the health inspector? When there were practically but few cases of typhoid fever in the city, the prediction was made that unless proper precautions were taken these cases would increase, and so they did. According to the newspapers there are 210 cases reported at present and how many more not reported we do not know. In this matter the government are just as lax as the city council and its health officer, because they do not bring their influence to compel the city authorities to do their duty.

The government has a large number of employees directly under the control of the Department of Public Works. I do not know that there is any provision for .furnishing pure water to the different departments of the government. I do know that there are a very large number of typhoid cases in this city? I understand that the epidemic has become so bad that the citizens have had to secure the old geological survey building as an emergency hospital. I do not know that the government can be held responsible altogether for the water of the city of Ottawa-
How can they be held responsible at all?

I do say that the government are responsible for the water their employees are consuming. And I say that, if there is any virtue in the sterilizing apparatus we have in the House of Commons, it is the duty of the government to furnish them to every department immediately. But, outside of this, there is the greater question. I believe the government exercises considerable influence on the city of Ottawa to-day. The government haS a contract with the city to furnish water for these buildings. The government has a right, as the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) says, to expect that pure water should be furnished. There is no doubt that, if the government had taken this matter in hand and had told the city plainly that if pure water was not furnished, the supply would be cut off and we would put in our own plant and the buildings supplied-
Where from?

That would be a question to be decided. We might take it from the same source, and do what the city of Ottawa should have done years ago-purify the water. I understand the city is making arrangements now for water purification. But those in charge of the government of the city of Ottawa have been derelict in

their duty to the citizens. Many precious lives have been sacrificed; many people are on sick beds who should not be there. I appeal to the Minister of Public Works, not so much as far as the city is concerned, but for the employees who, in this matter, are directly under his charge, and who cannot come to this House of Commons and raise their voices in protest against the water supplied to them. Every department is running the same danger that the citizens are running of drinking water from the Ottawa river, which is little better than sewage. The minister asks why the citizens do not boil the water. I am not a scientist, but I venture to say that boiling the water is not a sure preventive of danger. If you boil a pail of sewage, how much better is it than it was before? By boiling you kill anything alive that is there, but I have grave doubts whether you remove all danger.
The best physicians say the microbes will be killed.

I do not agree with the Minister of Public Works. A few days ago I rvas laid up, and feared an attack of typhoid. I told my physician who attended me that we were taking the precaution of boiling the water, and he said: ' If you boil a pair of sewage, does it make it any purer? You kill anything that is alive, but you do not purify it.'
Microbes have life; surely if you kill them you get rid-
I would like to see the government have a little life on this question.
We have been trying to kill the microbes.

I say, in conclusion, that this is no laughing matter, but a very serious one. If the cost is $10,000 or $500,000, to provide pure water for the employees of this government, the honour of the country is at stake, and it ought to be done and done immediately.

The Minister of Public Works asks how the government can do anything. The government has a contract with the city for a supply of water. If the city persists in supplying sewage, the minister can indict the council for maintaining a common nuisance. This would call the attention of these gentlemen to the fact that they have something to do besides self-advertising. I did not intend to speak on this point; I rose, in-the first place, to help the minister out on the question of supplying pure water. But, when he asks what he can do, I tell him he can indict these people for maintaining a common nuisance.

I have listened with interest to the discussion, and am glad to hear the expressions of sympathy from hop. members with the sufferers in this typhoid epidemic. The question, to my mind, is one for the mayor and corporation of the city of Ottawa. I regret that, for the past three or four months, there has been such a difference of opinion among the experts as to leave one at present quite at a loss as to avoidance of the danger. It has arisen only within the last two or three weeks, owing, no doubt, to the exceedingly low water in the Ottawa river from which the supply is drawn. It would have been quite impossible for the government or any one else to advise the city council when, apparently, the experts were at odds themselves as to the best course to be followed. But, since this very serious outbreak, every precaution, as I understand it, has been taken to do away with the poisonous condition of the water
By whom?

I am not a technical man in this matter, but I understand that some chemical preparation is to be mixed with the water which will purify it.
So far as holding the-government responsible is concerned, the responsibility seems to me to rest entirely on the shoulders of the corporation of the city of Ottawa. The fact has already been mentioned that the government has given the use of the geological survey building as a temporary hospital. I may explain that, the moment we learned there was need of more room, the chairman of the board of health, the medical health officer and I went to see the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) on this matter. That hon. gentleman at once gave his consent to the use of the building, and hastened matters in every way to place it at the city's disposal. And the same was true of the Militia Department in trying to help out. I can only say-in common, I am sure, with all members of this House-how deeply I regret that this outbreak has occurred in this city which has always tried to carry out any obligations into which it has entered with the government.

I do not find fault with the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. McGiv-erin) in seeking to whitewash the government. I was not blaming the government until the minister asked what he could do. I think he could do a good deal. For years, we have been reading how gentlemen in this city have protested again and again against the threatened contamination of the city water. But the mayor and corporation declared that the water was the finest in the world-everything around Ottawa was the finest in the world. As a matter of fact, Ottawa has been drinking the sewage of Pembroke, Almonte, Arnprior, Alymer

and all these other towns on the river. How the people of Ottawa have escaped trouble so long I cannot tell. However, the main thing is that the minister should notify the city that we want puTe water, he has a contract with the city. Let him notify the mayor that the city must supply these buildings with pure water. Let him for once put down his foot firmly, while at the same time maintaining his genial countenance.

I would suggest that the minister tell the city that, he will not ask this item to be carried because the city is not fulfilling their contract. When they are giving us poisonous water to drink they are not giving us what their contract was supposed to call for. When the minister notifies the' city that he will not carry this item of $115,000 otherwise, he will be doing something to get pure water. I do not believe for one minute that the city of Ottawa cannot get pure water, and the minister can help the city get pure water if he refuses to pay them this $115,000 until it is supplied us.
I think the minister could iijring a little pressure to bear on the city by letting this item stand.
This iteifi has nothing to do with pure water.
Does the minister want to drive us to drink something else?
I would be awfully sorry.
On behalf of the members of this House I would suggest that the minister has the remedy in his hands by having an emergency consultation with Hiram Walker.
Will the hon. gentleman be the chief executive officer at the conference?

I see that the firm of A.
K.	Mills & Son, Ottawa, have received $5,866 for plumbing, &c., last year. Was any of this work done after public competition?
That was for the supply and installation of marble lavatories.
That is only one item in a total of $25,866.

That was jobbing work, there were no tenders invited. It could not be done very well 'by tender. If you take an old building and tear out the old lavatories and put in new ones, it is something that you cannot do satisfactorily by tender. If I were doing it for myself I would not think of calling for tenders, but would try and get good reliable men. Any one doing it by tender would be sure
to exact a large margin for unexpected difficulties.
Ottawa Departmental Buildings-Langevin Block-new boilers and alterations in heating apparatus, $5,000.

$5,000 of this is a revote. It is to make provision for replacing four boilers in the Langevin block on the east side, also to complete necessary changes in connection with the heating apparatus. It was done by public competition, after advertisement in the newspapers of Ottawa.
In how many newspapers was this advertisement inserted?
It'could not have been in a great many, because it only cost $35 for advertising. I presume it was in one of the Ottawa papers.	-
Perhaps the chief architect could tell in which one.
He does not remember in what paper it was advertised. It is done through the secretary of the department.
Was this put in two or three papers?

I think I can safely say there would only be one.
Mr. BLAIN- Which one?

If in only one, it would be the * Free Press.' But if it was in any of the others, I cannot tell which. I will give my hon. friend a list of the papers in which it was published.	.
Ottawa Parliament	Buildings-improvements, $10,000.

That is to make provision for general improvements to the interior of the parliament buildings and the library. I can tell what was done last year : Tiling the library, $4,025 ; partitions, $1,450 ; ventilation, $800 ; plumbing, $453 ; furniture, $653 ; painting and gilding tower and roof, $600.
Will that have to be done every year ?
Practically the same amount is expended every year.
Is it spent simply because the money is voted every year or simply because it is necessary ?
It is actually necessary.
It seems strange that the gilding and painting in the library that the hon. gentleman has mentioned have to be done every year.
No, this is to the interior of the building and the library.
Do the interior of the building and the library require to be painted every year ?
No. but there are painting, gilding and other improvements necessary to keep the buildings in repair.

What is proposed to be done with regard to providing more suitable accommodation for the library than we have at present ? The library is so crowded both in the basement and on the general floor that it is very inconvenient both to the members and to those engaged in it. In fact, I find it very difficult to get much satisfaction in the library because three times out of four, you cannot get anything you want. There is a general complaint that everything is bundled together and there seems to be no possibility of any system or order being evolved out of it, so that one can go and get anything he wants. There is a number of people in the library, but if you send in a hurry or go in yourself you cannot get what you want sometimes in three or four days and sometimes cannot get it at all. For years it has been apparent that there was urgent need for increased accommodation and the government state year after year that they intend to take it up, but we have not yet any distinct information from them as to what is contemplated.

I am very glad that my hon. friend has mentioned this question which certainly is one of a good deal of importance, owing to the very crowded condition of the library. The matter was mentioned last year and certain suggestions were made to me. One was that an additional story should be put on to cover a portion of the building that is now occupied by the reading room and that we should also extend the library so as to take in the room which is occupied by my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham), and also the members' smoking room. In that way additional accommodation might be given. Another idea is to erect an additional wing to the eastward in connection with the Senate part of the building. The question of the relative expense of the two modes of affording accommodation has been talked of. Another idea which has been suggested is to erect another building towards the edge of the cliff which would be used as a stack room and have a tunnel connecting the present library with that building. All these are under consideration, and it is expected that the Speaker of the Senate and the other nfem,bers of the Library Committee will very soon have a meeting at which the chief architect and myself shall be present to go quite fully into the whole matter. I have an idea myself, which is entirely my personal idea, Mr. PUGSLEY.
that it is worthy of consideration whether we should not carry out a wing, say, from the western side of the building for the purpose of affording a new chamber for the members of the House where there would be perfect ventilation on each side and which would be open to the pure air of heaven and then utilize this chamber for purposes in connection with the library and reading room. I have that idea; I do not know whether it is worthy of consideration or not, but I do not like the idea of having a couple of hundred people who are constantly in attendance in this chamber in addition to the spectators in the galleries, shut off from direc^ ventilation and from the open, free air. I do not know whether it is worthy of seriously considering or net.
I hope you will develop it.
That would be a much better arrangement than we have now.

I never could understand why files of newspapers ten or twelve years old, are kept piled up in the library from year to year. Why could they not be put in some room >
They are not wanted very often and they are taking up the best space in that building.
That is for the Library Committee to decide.

Then I take it that I am correct in saying that nothing has been done up to the present except talk. This talk has been going on for years. It seems to me that it is time that somebody got busy, and did a little more than talk. The process of evolution has been so slow that I think we will all be dead before there is a new library if we do not do more than has been done lately.

I have no control over the Library Committee, but I certainly do think that they ought to have these files of old papers removed. I do not see any necessity for them. I quite agree with the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) that there is no reason why they should be kept there taking up room in the library. I do not know whether they are kept there to emphasize the necessity of additional accommodation or not-I do not suggest that-but that is the effect of it because everybody feels upon going in there that something ought to be done. I think the first thing that ought to be done is for the Library Committee to order these files of old newspapers to be removed because there is no need of keeping them there.
Ottawa parliament buildings, driveway pavement, $20,000.

We have put down pavement on the driveways all around the parliament grounds.
, Mr. LANCASTER. Is that not an enormous price? It must have been paved with silver dollars.
No.
What was the total cost?

From the 1st April, 1910, to 30th November, 1910, we paid to the Ottawa Construction Company $5,000, to T. S. Kirby for broken stone, $2,439.03, for stone, sand and cement $3,436, and for labour $5,904.03. The appropriation was $21,000 and that left an unexpended balance of $4,220.81 on the 30th November.
That is about $17,000. How many yards, or miles, of surface did that cover?

That was applied in laying pavements around the east and west blocks, square facing on Wellington street, and covering the roadway in front of the House of Commons. There were 8,000 superficial yards of pavement altogether. It is a very nice pavement.

It ought to be a very nice pavement at the price of $2 a yard. Does the hon. gentleman not seriously think this is an exorbitant price to pay for putting a roadway in condition? If the hon. gentleman would take that before any ordinary road builders in any province he would have difficulty in explaining such an expenditure.
How deep did they dig?	,
There was about eight . inches of solid concrete put down and it was covered over with asphalt.

Has the hon. gentleman ever compared this with any work done by municipalities or other institutions that are constructing these roads in every province? I think that is a most extravagant price to pay.
This was done by day work under a competent foreman.

The different counties of Ontario do similar work to this, and I do not believe they pay any such prices. Has inquiry been made to ascertain what prices are paid for similar work by other public bodies?
About five years ago we invited tenders for the work on Wellington street, and it cost us $2.49 per yard.
Was it the same class of work?

About the same. There is a great variation in the character of this work, and I understand it runs from $1.80 in some localities up to $2.50. When you come to a permanent pavement for a driveway, which is on a slope, and you have to put eight inches of solid concrete I do not think the cost is too great.
Why was this done by day work instead of by contract, as formerly?
Who was the foreman?
Mr. Baxter, an employee of the department, and an experienced man.

I should think it would be a great relief to the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. McGiverin) if this were done by contract, because it must be a great deal of trouble to him to supply the workmen for day labour. I wonder if it was the influence of the hon. member (Mr. McGiverin) who caused the minister to change the system from contract to day labour. I should think that the city of Ottawa would be a dangerous place to experiment in doing work for day labour.
The work was done by the permanent staff, with the addition of a few extra men. We had a competent foreman. and I believe the work was done as economically as possible, and it is well done.
Is this not what is commonly known as tar macadam?
No; it is an asphalt composition.
There is not very heavy traffic around these grounds, and I should think it would not be necessary to do 'the work as it has been done.

There is a great deal of driving, and I suppose the chief architect thought it was better to make a good job of it at once.
At six o'clock, House took recess.
After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.
House in committee on Bill (No. 44) respecting the Lachine, Jacques Cartier and Maisonneuve Railway.-Mr. Geoffrion.
On section 4,

subsubtopic: LACHINE, JACQUES CARTIER AND MAISONNEUVE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
I have an amendment to offer to section 4 of the Bill. The amendment is not important, and I understand the committee have power to accept it, waiving the rule. The effect of the amendment is to give the company power to connect its line with the Canadian Pacific railway and the Canadian Northern railway. The amendment provides:
Subject to the approval of the Commission the company may connect its line of railway with the Canadian Pacific railway and the Canadian Northern railway.

subsubtopic: LACHINE, JACQUES CARTIER AND MAISONNEUVE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: We have usually followed the course in the Railway Committee of giving the company power to amalgamate with such lines as are set out in the Bill. This was not done in this case, and, therefore, following the usual custom, it should not be done in the House. It is an important amendment and no notice has been given.

subsubtopic: LACHINE, JACQUES CARTIER AND MAISONNEUVE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: If there is an objection, of course I shall have to give notice of the amendment, and will ask the committee to report progress and ask leave to sit again.

subsubtopic: LACHINE, JACQUES CARTIER AND MAISONNEUVE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I would like to be informed of the route of this railway. Section 1 declares that a railway authorized by the legislature of Quebec, which would therefore be regarded as provincial in its character, shall now be declared a railway for the general advantage of Canada. Personally, I am opposed to putting in that declaration unless there is some evidence before the committee that the road is of rather a national character and not simply local.

subsubtopic: LACHINE, JACQUES CARTIER AND MAISONNEUVE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: In the committee I objected to the principle of taking over these provincial lines and bringing them under federal jurisdiction without some strong reason, because there are often provisions in the provincial Bill that we destroy by making the railway a federal line, thus bringing it under another authority and jurisdiction. We had the same thing last year in connection with Ontario railways. By taking them under our jurisdiction we removed them from the control of the Railway Commission of Ontario. That occurred in connection with telegraph and telephone lines. Then there was the other objection which the Minister of Public Works has raised. We have of late years made it a rule to compel the party who desired to have a provincial railway declared to be for the general advantage of Canada to give some specific and justifiable ground for making the declaration which transfers the road from the control of the one to the other. But in this case even the local Act was not looked up. The discussion was hurried through and little time was given to it.

subsubtopic: LACHINE, JACQUES CARTIER AND MAISONNEUVE RAILWAY COMPANY.
LACHINE, JACQUES CARTIER AND MAISONNEUVE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I was not present when the Bill was before the committee. We generally discuss those features to. which my hon. friend refers pretty thoroughly, but he was present and says they were not thoroughly discussed. I plead guilty to being quite partial to putting all the railways possible under Dominion jurisdiction, on account of the control we thus get over the traffic, which is conceded to be very complete under our Board of Railway Commissioners. The point has been raised during the past year, in fact a case is now in progress, in which it is contended that even where a provincial line connects^ with a Dominion line the Dominion Railway Commission has no power to even regulate the through rates on that part of the line which has a provincial charter. This makes it all the more necessary, even to control through rates, that we should have jurisdiction. If my hon. friend will give notice that he is going to move this amendment and let that stand until the next meeting of the committee, the promoter will be here.

subsubtopic: LACHINE, JACQUES CARTIER AND MAISONNEUVE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: There was a discussion about that in the committee and the provincial statute was turned up to see where it differed and I understand an amendment was added in sections 3 and 4.

subsubtopic: LACHINE, JACQUES CARTIER AND MAISONNEUVE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I was under the impression that instructions were given to have the names of those other railways with which this one is connected inserted in the Bill. The committee will remember that Mr. Wainwright came before the Railway Committee, and said that they were extremely anxious tlhe Bill should go through in order t<x give them a connecting link between the Grand Trunk railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific. So urgent was the demand that there was no apposition, and his request was granted.

speechtext:
I think that was in connection with another Bill entirely.
