House in committee on Bill (No. 32) to incorporate the Security Trusts Corporation. -Mr. Martin (Regina).
This Bill was considered toy the Committee on Banking and Commerce.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have no knowledge of the Bill, tout if it has received the consideration of the Committee on Banking and Commerce, I shall not object. If there be any abjection, I shall toe glad to look into it. No doubt the committee gave it very careful consideration.

The consideration of the . committee was largely ^long the same lines as that of a Bill we passed the year before last, about which there was a good deal of controversy. I think it was the Bill of the Prudential Loan and Trust Company. There is one amendment that, in my opinion, should be made that does not appear in the Bill. It should be a part of all Bills to incorporate trust or loan companies, insurance companies-though it does not apply so much to these-as banking companies. It should be provided that whenever such a company becomes possessed of money or valuable consideration which does not belong to the company, but for which there are no claimants and no heirs, that property should be transferred to the state. At present these companies treat such moneys practically as their own. It was urged by the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) that this provision should be in a general'Bill. I think it would be natural to have it in a general Bill, but, in the meantime, I think we should make it a part of every special Bill of this kind. Of course, I am not going to try to stop the Bill for the purpose of making this amendment, but I draw' the attention of the Minister of Finance to the matter. No individual is allowed to do what these corporations do-appropriate money which does not belong to them because they happen to become possessed of it and no heir or claimant is found. If the property were real estate, it would pass, under the law of escheat, to the province.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does not that apply to personal property?

In connection with real estate the province of Ontario has asserted its clftim in some such cases. And, in the case of personal property held by individuals, it passes to the_ state, but I am not aware of instances in which this rule was applied to these companies.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I find that the law clerk has made a memorandum that one of these sections is not so carefully drawn as it should be. I suggest that we allow this Bill to stand, and the points raised can be inquired into before it comes up for consideration again.

I would call the attention of the Minister of Finance to subsection 3 of section 6 which reads:
3. The company may, by by-law, provide that a resolution in writing signed by all the directors shall be valid as if it had been passed at a meeting of the directors.
That practically does away with the holding of directors' meetings and I do not think this sort of thing should be encouraged. The business is supposed to be directed by the joint action of directors, after
consultation. But, if the matter be left in this shape, each director practically becomes a rubber stamp for the manager. And we find that that is the origin of trouble in many of these cases. I think that such a provision should not be in any of these Bills.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think that similar provision is to be found in other Bills. I cannot recall the particular case, but I recollect the question being before the committee, and the argument was put forward that, in matters of no very great concern, it was found inconvenient to get the Board of Directors together, and the convenient way was to send a memorandum round and have each director sign the resolution. And I have known that to be done in graver bodies in cases of emergency. Of course, it might be difficult to draw the line between matters requiring conference and matters more of routine requiring merely the formal approval of the board. I will bear in mind the suggestion, which is in the direction of safety and prudence, and will call the attention of the law officers who advise us in such matters to the observations of the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Haggart).

I drew attention to this matter in the committee, and thought that the provision had been struck out. I thought and still think, that the provision is a bad one. The reason urged in its favour is the difficulty of getting the board together. But this is a trust company belonging to one province so that its directors are not scattered so far that they could not be got together for the companies business. I have seen the working of this law in one or two instances where, had it not been checked in proper time, it would have been likely to do great harm. When it is proposed that the 'board should take certain action, a paper is prepared and sent to each director with all the reasons that can be advanced why the resolution should be signed at once and sent on. There is usually some plea of urgency and some intimation of pending loss if the action proposed be not taken. The memorandum does not bring out all the facts that would be brought out in a discussion at a board meeting. But the individual director dislikes to burk or check the proposed action, and so, instead of directing, as a director is supposed to do, he signs and sends the resolution on. The effect is to give power into the hands of a small executive. I think it is a bad provision, and should not be allowed in these Bills.

The objections to this provision were not overlooked in the committee. The section was fully considered before being adopted. We thought there was a sufficient safeguard in the fact

that all the directors-not a majority only -have to sign in these cases. If the same question were brought before the board, it might be brought before a bare quorum a majority of whom would carry. We thought that the proviso that every director's name should be signed would be an equal safeguard. We came to the conclusion that we would allow the clause to go through, because it had gone through if I am not mistaken, in the case of the Prudential, a Bill that as I understood the matter, had received very careful consideration in the committee and had been made something of a model Bill. But having adopted that Bill only a year or two ago, it was thought well to allow this clause to go through.

I think the hon. gentleman's arguments are neither strong nor sound. I do not think you will analyse any question that is presented before a board as well by sending it to one individual with all the arguments on one side and more on the other, no board is doing its duty which does this. In the first case you are more likely to make the directors figure-heads than intelligent and useful officials. Take the Farmers' Bank, how easy it would have been to pass something around like that. The manager, who seemed to dominate everything, could get it signed.
How much good would it do to have a meeting?

That a certain number of men there did not attend to their duties was not on account of the fact that they did not meet but because they didn't do their duty when they did meet. But if they desired to pass around something, would it not be more easy to do it if there had been only a few sharp men on the board? I know one party that had to make two trips to New York to safeguard the interest of himself and friends on account of a provision such as that, made foolishly or maliciously by the manager and one or two of the members of the board who were acting in concert with him, and who stood to benefit if it was carried through. The result was that he was endangering the financial interests of all the members of that board and of that company. If it had not been burked they would have suffered a serious loss.

I am not sure but that I may say that the hon. gentleman's arguments are neither strong nor sound, as he characterized mine. Now, I still submit that with a board of four, which you could have with this comnany, because that would be a majority of the seven, the smallest number of directors, you might have on that board a very strong minded man who was sufficiently persuasive to induce the other members of the board to come to Mr. HENDERSON.
his opinion. If you sent the motion around to the various directors, and let them sit down in their quiet and reflective moments, and consider the whole question for themselves, I am not sure but that you would get a much better judgment than you could where you had one strong minded man dominating the rest. I still hold that the opinion expressed by the committee was wise and sound.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There is a motion that the committee rise.
My hon. friend from Hal-ton (Mr. Henderson) expresses my view3 completely.

Before the committee rises, I want to ask an explanation of section 15. [DOT] There is a section in this Bill which provides that this company may do business throughout Canada, but subject to the laws of the province, and if there is any conflict, the laws of the province shall prevail. Now, I do not think we are doing our duty in this parliament to incorporate a company and then say that its powers shall not be exercised if they happen to conflict with the law of any province. That i3 not good legislation.
I think that is a good clause. You would fiot want to enact anything in one province that was in conflict with the laws of that province.
But let not the province enact a provincial law which is in conflict with a Dominion statute.
The Act respecting the Observance of the Lord's Day is based upon that principle exactly.

I think perhaps that was a law of an exceptional character. But here we are claiming jurisdiction to incorporate this company for Dominion purposes, with power to do business throughout Canada, and yet the effect of this would be that in one province they could do certain things, and in another province they would not have the same power ; their power might be different in each of the provinces of Canada. If we have authority to incorporate this company with power to do business throughout Canada, then we should not make it subject to the laws of each particular province in which it might happen to be carrying on business.

What would happen if, when your Bill became law, a province should make a law of their own saying that you should not do business in that province unless you complied with certain provisions of their law?

I should say that their law was void unless there was a question

of taxation. They might impose a tax on the company, as they do. But any statute *which attempted to interfere with the larger rights which this parliament gave to a company, would, I think, be ultra vires of the provincial legislature. But here we assume to pass an Act, and then we say that it may be picked to pieces in any province.
We have done the same thing to-day with an insurance company.

There has been a case under consideration as to the powers of a provincial legislature to incorporate a company to do business throughout Canada. But here there is no question of our authority to incorporate this company. But we are saying that although we give you such rights, these rights must be exercised subject to any law of any province, and if there is any conflict with that, the provincial law shall prevail.
I understand there is a stated case being sent to the Privy Council to determine the respective rights of a province and the Dominion in case of conflict. There may be concurrent jurisdiction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That the Bill might involve possible conflict between the province and the Dominion is something that I have not had before me. It strikes me, as it is read by the Minister of Public Works, that the earlier part of the clause as to doing business subject to the laws of the province, might mean that inasmuch as trustee laws are under the jurisdiction of a province as dealing with property and civil rights, in the exercise of their functions as a trust corporation they have to bear in mind that trusts are regulated by the province and not by the Dominion. The law of trusteeship is a provincial law, and I think the intention must be that they should carry out the provincial law. They would become a corporate company for trustee business, but they would have to do their business subject to the law of the province as respects trusteeships. I think that is what it is intended to mean. The latter part of the clause respecting possible conflict, is more serious.

In some places.

I am obliged to the minister for his consideration. expenditure will receive fair consideration from this side. But the difficulty is we do not know what is his policy, and he does not seem to know it himself. Therefore, we are not able to apply a fair test to his expenditures.

was made on a previous occasion, rose in his place and denied that he had made any such statement. The hon member (Mr. Armstrong) is bound to accept that denial, and I have no doubt he will accept it cheerfully.

The matter had been under the consideration of the government foT some months, and we had made up our minds to erect a public building. What was wrong in the Prime Minister, at a time when no election was pending, and every reason to suppose that the appropriation would be made long before an election, telling the people that he was impressed with the necessity of a post office, and would ask the Minister of Public Works to provide for one? Not quite all. At the same meeting, when the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) said whatever he did say, the Prime Minister corrected him, and put the-
That is denied.

I have said it in the presence of the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid ' Laurier), and he did not deny it, and will not dare to deny it, and I do not propose to take a denial at second-hand from the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley).
The member for Pictou denied it.

But the Prime Minister has neveT denied it. He corrected the matter going to the public press, and said that if they got only what they deserved they would not get a public building, but he would be more generous, and deal with them better than they deserved.

has been seriously brought to his attention. If the hon. gentleman would draw it to his attention I am sure the Prime Minister would feel it of sufficient importance to refer to it.

I repeat what.I said. It would do less harm to the country if he frankly admitted that he was governed by the political complexion of the member of the constituency.
I asked him a few moments ago whether he would say that if the people of the riding of North Grey, at the next election, returned a supporter of the government.

his attitude rvould be at all altered with respect to a public building in Meaford, and he answered that he always avoided giving promises. East Grey and North Grey have items, tout South Grey has no item. I think the item for East Grey has been put in the estimates since the election of 1908. The minister would know if I am correct.

I have not the estimates for the previous years here. I may say that I sometimes have a feeling that I am doing even more for constituencies represented' by our friends opposite, than I ought to do; and a good deal of fault is found with me by some of our. friends because they do not get the public buildings to which they think they are entitled and they blame me for erecting public buildings in constituencies represented by our opponents; Sometimes it makes it more difficult for me to give grants in constituencies represented by hon. gentlemen opposite, when I find them so lacking in appreciation. In an election which took place a short time ago down in Nova Scotia, one hon. member sitting on the other side of the House went there and claimed credit for every item of public expenditure which had been made in the county, he said he was entitled to credit for it
Who was it ?

The hon. member for Digiby (Mr. Jameson). He claimed the entire credit for grants which had been made, grants to wharfs and other improvements. I have that upon authority so strong that I must give all credit to it.
When did that take place ?

Six ot eight weeks ago. 'That hon. gentleman went upon the platform and denied to the government, denied to me, denied to our supporters any credit for these improvements, and claimed that he was entitled to the entire credit for them all. It is conduct such as this by our friends opposite that makes it a little harder for me sometimes to grant them all the improvements they ask for.
In the absence of the hon. member for Digiby, I think I would be safe in denying that he made any such assertion, or claimed all the credit.
That is my information.
As the hon. member for Digby is not here it seems to me that this is an assertion that the minister is not entitled to make.
We will come to the Nova Scotia items for wharfs and the hon. member for Digby will have the fullest opportunity of speaking on the question.
We have just sent for him now.
Are all the expenditures which have been made in the riding since the hon. member for Digby was elected, proper expenditures?
Yes, every one.
Were these expenditures asked for by the hon. member for Digby?
A number were asked for by our own friends as well.
The hon. gentleman would be perfectly justified in asking for the expenditures which have been made in that riding?
Yes.
Then, what fault has the hon. minister to find with the hon. member for Digby?

I will tell the hon gentleman. Instead of the hon. member for Digby getting up on the platform and saying that the Minister of Public Works has -expended public money wisely and properly in his constituency and in the public interest, the hon. gentleman got up and told the people that the government was not entitled to the slightest credit. I see that the hon. member for Digby is now in his place and I will repeat the statement that I made. I was saying a short time ago that it made it a little more difficult than it would otherwise be because hon. gentlemen opposite are in the habit of going through their constituencies and claiming the sole credit for public expenditures made by the government, and I had in my Mr. MEIGHEN.
mind more especially the hon. member for Digby, who, I was informed, went upon different platforms in the last local election in Digby, claimed for himself the entire credit of the expenditures which had been made by the government in the county of Digby and contended that the government and the friends of the government were not entitled to any credit at all but that he and he alone had succeeded in getting these moneys expended in the county. That was the statement I was making, and what I said in the absence of the hon. gentleman was that I did not think that that was a course that hon. members opposite ought to take. If the expenditure is wise the government ought to be given the credit for it.
I supnose it was public money that was expended?

Clearly public money that was expended. In my own judgment it is entirely a misconception on the part of an hon. member * of the opposition to say, that because he makes a representation to the minister, the minister considers the representations along with the representations of others, and an amount is put in the estimates, he is entitled to claim all the credit of it.

If a constituency is represented by one of the minister's own political friends and public money is expended in that constituency, is the representative entitled to the credit, or is the Minister of Public Works?
The government is entitled to the credit of it.
Not the representative?	.

The representative, as a supporter of the government, when he goes to the people, claims credit for the government and claims that the public ought to support the government. But the hon. gentleman in one breath stated:	I
am entitled to the credit for these expenditures, but the government is not entitled to any credit.

Then the minister acknowledges that it is the proper principle for his candidates to go to a constituency and say:	You should support the
government because they have spent a certain amount of money in your constituency?
It is fair to say that.
That is what I call bribery in the different constituencies.

Mr. Chairman, as the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) has referred to me personally in the House, it is only right that under the circumstances

I should make some remarks on the subject, With regard to these expenditures which are being made in Digby and with regard to the appropriations placed in the estimates for that purpose, the minister very well knows that I drew his attention on several occasions, personally and by correspondence, to the necessity of these works. I had the pleasure of several interviews with the minister and I also had considerable correspondence with him on the subject. I do not think that I ever asked for an expenditure that was not perfectly warranted by the facts and necessities of the case. I furthermore think there were many instances to which I might refer in which the minister did not comply with the requests that were made in that behalf. But the minister has gone further and has said that upon public platforms I have claimed the entire credit for these votes. The minister is labouring under a misconception. On the contrary, it was the gentlemen who were opposed to me and to the Conservative candidate in Digby who thus claimed the entire credit. It was my duty to myself, it was my duty to the constituency which I have the honour td represent, to, in so far as I could, rectify that misconception and counteract those influences. I did not begin it, nor did I begin the discussion with regard to these public works in Digby or the votes made therefor. I did not do so because I did not think it was a question which should enter into a local election, but when I noticed that gentlemen who were opposed to the Conservative candidate were going about the county of Digby and asserting that they and not I had made the representations upon the strength of which these votes were made and these public works were going to be undertaken, I felt it was my duty, to set the matter right. I also understand that these gentlemen were exhibiting letters from the Minister of Public Works himself, stating that it was upon their representations that these votes were placed in the estimates. I thereupon took the correspondence which I had had with the hon. minister, and I also took the different issues of * Hansard ' which referred to these matters when they were brought up in the House, and I read them, as I considered it was my duty to read them before the electors of Digby. It was not I who projected this question into the local election. I did not think it was altogether proper, I thought it was entirely out of place, but when the question was raised by gentlemen on the other side and when they sought to detract in every way possible from the efforts of myself as a Conservative sitting in this House and representing the county of Digbjq I thought it was only right and proper to set the matter right. The minister seems if I gauge properly the state of mind in which
he was when I entered the House, to have been a little irritated.
Not at all.
I am glad to know that
Not a bit.

Because I do not think the minister has any reason whatever to object to a statement of bald facts and facts, which are borne out by the records, on the part of any man who has the honour to represent a constituency in this parliament. The statement which I made upon every occasion was simply that these were the facts as disclosed by the records, .that in so far as I was personally concerned I was perfectly satisfied that any gentleman who had assisted should have the credit to which he was entitled, but that I also, as the one who had brought these matters to the attention of the minister and the House,, felt that I was entitled to credit, in so far as the records disclosed my efforts in that, particular regard. I do not think that the-minister, when he hears this explanation from me, will question the propriety of what I did. If this question, which came up on that occasion should arise again, I should do exactly the same thing under similar circumstances.

I rather was given to understand that the hon. gentleman had denied- credit to anybody else, but that he had claimed the whole credit for himself. Did the hon. gentleman give due credit to the Minister of Public Works for these useful public works that he was having done in the county?

The minister has stated what he understood to be a fact, namely, that I had denied credit to any person else, and he also has asked me whether or not I gave credit to the Minister of Public Works. I do not know that I said in so many words that the Minister of Public Works was entitled to any particular credit for this expenditure of public moneys in Digby, or for the votes made for that purpose, but I certainly read the correspondence between the minister and myself, my own letters to the minister and the minister's reply to me. I also quoted from ' Hansard,' in which my statements were reported, and the statements of the minister in reply, and I allowed the electors of the county of Digby and others present to draw their own conclusions. I merely did that because it had been put up to me that I had done nothing whatever in the way of assisting to get these works, or urging their necessity on the minister. I did not begin it; it was begun by my political opponents, and I only displayed the records in self-defence, so that the people might understand how matters really stood.

The hon. gentleman from Wellington (Mr. Martin) said there had been a considerable expenditure of public money in East Grey, and he instanced the expenditure of $1,000 in Thorn-bur.y to repair a wharf. I would remind him that that is the only appropriation in these estimates for East Grey. I think the work is needed; I am not complaining about it, and even though the amount is small, the people will be grateful for it.
No one suggests the hon. gentleman would complain of an expenditure there.

No, but in the county of Wellington no less than four of these public buildings have been erected or are . under way in small villages, some of them within two or three miles of each other when there are large counties in which there is no expenditure on public buildings at all. It would seem to me that is due to the fact that the county of Wellington is represented in this House by three Reformers and that the other counties happen to be represented by Conservatives. I think the comparison I make is a fair one. Further, I do not think that the amount proposed to be expended in East Grey, in Thornbury, $1,000, is likely to influence the electors one way or the other.

I was not finding fault with the expenditure of public money in East Grey or in Wellington, but I cited it to show that the arguments of hon. gentlemen opposite that money was being promised to influence voters on the eve of an election, was not correct. I do not think any man could imagine that the money expended in Thornbury could carry the election against the hon. member for East Grey, and I do not think that item was in the estimates until after the election of 1908.

It strikes me very forcibly that the Minister of Public Works has shown us very clearly to-night what his idea is in trying to administer this' department. I was very much astonished at some of the remarks he made, not because we did not know that was the way he looked at things, but because we did not expect him to acknowledge it. He sets to work and he asks the hon. member for Digby if he gave the Minister of Public Works CTedit for making improvements in 't)he countv of Digby, and he also gets up in this House and states that he thinks the government of the country ought to have the credit 'for these improvements in that constituency. Surely the Minister of Public Works knows that the people of this country think that he is spending their money and not the Grit money of this country. And when the minister erects public build-Mr. JAMESON
ings in any constituency he is supposed to erect them on some principle and in the public interest, but to-night he has acknowledged to us right here that he is using the machinery of the Public Works Department practically for the purpose of trying to bribe the various constituencies in this country. We have felt all along that that is the principle on which he decides where he will carry on public works in this country. We see, before the elections, hundreds of appropriations brought down for public works that are left over from year to year, and we find such items in the appropriations for Ontario, which are now before us. We have items here revoted every year since 1908, which were put in by the government as the minister himself says, in order that the government might have credit for building the works in these constituencies, and so that the government might be able to get the people to vote for their candidates. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that it is an extraordinary thing for a minister of the Crown in this country to get up and claim that he and the government should have credit for building public works in any constituency, and should appeal to the voters of the country to vote for his party because he has done so. I would like to ask you, Mr. Chairman, if any one could possibly make a balder statement as to the attempt to bribe the constituencies of this country by means of public works erected by the expenditure of the money belonging to all the people of Canada,

It is all very well for my hon. friend to talk that way. Suppose there is a public work that he thinks is needed in a constituency and the government does not build it, surely he would blame the government, and on the other hand surely it is not an unreasonable recognition of what the government does, if in any constituency it has met the* public requirements so as to encouragef trade by the improvement of harbours or1 the building of wharfs; surely it is not unreasonable to suppose that a member of the opposition going on the public platform who claims credit for getting that work done, should say: So far as this constituency is concerned I recognize that the government has met the reasonabld demands of the public and has done in this respect what ought to be done for' the advancement of the interests of the people, and in meeting their just and reasonable demands. What I object to is that a member of the opposition should claim credit to himself when certain things are done, while at the same time he condemns the government for things that do not happen to be done.
Who did that?
We had that story and, we do not want it over again.
It was denied.

I object to the principle laid down by the Minister of Public Works in this regard. If the Minister of Public Works would adopt some principle in expending the money under his control with regard to distributing it throughout the country in places most) needing it, according to their size and the revenues they contribute, irrespective of who represents these constituencies, there would be no objection. If the minister should go to the people after the election and say: I have administered my department fairly and honestly for the benefit of all the people of Canada, then he could take credit to himself for administering his department wisely. But, it is neither right nor just that the minister should go into a particular constituency and say: You are a community of 700 or 800 people, I have given you a building to which you were not entitled in fair play, and therefore you should vote for this government-That is not proper.
I would never say they w'ere not entitled to it.

I take exception to the views expressed by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Perley), and I do not know that he realizes himself what he did say. He made the statement that the Minister of Public Works had come here to-night, that he had put these items on the estimates for the very purpose

Mr. PERLEY'. I did not say that.
I took your words down.
Read them; you haven't got them there at all.

The hon. gentleman stated that these items were put in the estimates for the purpose of getting the support of the people for the government candidates. If the hon. gentleman did not make that statement, and if he denies that he did, I will have to take his word.

I know the hon. gentleman does not want to be unfair. What I said was that the Minister of Public Works said that when he erected buildings in a community he and the government should have credit for so doing, and what his statement practically meant was that when the elections came on the people should vote for him on that account.

What I said was if the government with respect to my constituency had done justice by that constituency, had acted fairly by it, had done what was reasonable and proper for the development !
of the place by the improvement of harbours, &c., it was only fair that the government should get reasonable credit for that.

I have to accept my hon. friend's explanation, but I fear that when some gentlemen speak, they perhaps go further than they intended to go. But hon. gentlemen know that they go on the platforms of this country and condemn the government for not having expended money in certain cases. I have never met one of them on the stump who did not take that ground. In the House every day attacks are made on the government for extravagant expenditure, for wasting money in building public works, wharfs, &c., which hon. gentlemen allege are not prudent expenditures; but when it comes to their own constituencies, every one of them has his hand out, every one is on his feet .pleading for some expenditure in his own riding. I do not think that is consistent. We have resolution after resolution submitted, condemning the expenditures of the government. Hon. gentlemen do not as a rule condemn any particular expenditure. I have been watching the proceedings of the House for some years but I have not seen hon. gentlemen moving to strike out this item or that item very often, they are very careful about that, they are afraid to put themselves on record as against this or that public undertaking, for which the government are spending money.
Was the hon. gentleman present the last time we were in supply, when we moved to strike out an item ?
I say there are few cases where hon. gentlemen do more to strike at a particular item.
The hon. gentlemen said never.

I did not say any such thing. There are a few cases where hon. gentlemen are very careful not to strike at any particular item and seldom if ever, condemn an item of expenditure in the constituency of a Conservative member.
In the very nature of things such items would not be likely to be subject to attack.

It is legitimate for hon. gentlemen to condemn the government for not having made any expenditure they think should have been made that has been voted, but it is just as fair for a government supporter to take credit to the government because the government did make expenditures which he and the electors think meritorious.
We are obliged for this lecture, but as a business man, would not the hon. member not condemn a manager of his, who would spend $25,000 on a building where a $5,000 building would do ?

If a superintendent of works represented that a foreman or manager in another department had expended $20,000 on a building that should have been erected for $5,000 and on investigation, I found that he had misrepresented and drawn on his imagination that he had no foundation in fact for his statement, I would dismiss the superintendent-and that is what the ridings of the hon. gentleman should do with them.

The hon. gentleman would condemn a man who, in building for him a building that should cost $5,000 or $6,000 placed a cupola on it and lined it with diamonds and gold and clocks, the' hon. gentleman knows that our objection to the heavy expenditure has never been proved unfounded. Last session I pointed out that if they took $100,000 and built ten post offices they would be doing more service to the country than by building only four post offices at $25,000 each.

A superintendent who in building a warehouse would add a cupola and line it with gold should be dismissed. My hon. friend knows that there has been no such case as that, that he was drawing on his imagination, that it is a mere fiction in the mind of my hon. friend.
The hon. gentleman does not know what he is talking about.
It might be economy to build substantial buildings as far as the money goes as otherwise they might have to be renewed.

Does the hon. gentleman say that as a rule, a town of 600 or 700 inhabitants needs a $10,000 post office? Why you would see such a post office long before you saw the rest of the village. At the same time there are places in the country going without buildings, producing ten times the revenue and progressing ten times as rapidly. The hon. gentleman talks about drawing on the imagination, can he find in his imagination any justification for a $10,000 or $12,000 edifice in a village of 600 inhabitants ? He knows quite well that a $5,000 building would be all that place would need for the next two or three decades.

This is all due to the partisanship which hon. gentlemen opposite introduced into the Public Works Department many years ago. Prior to the election of 1900, one of the ministers then in office sent out a private circular addressed Mr. CONMEE.
to the Reform candidates all over Canada. I have a copy of that circular in my hands but shall not read it as it has been put on ' Hansard ' in former discussions. The first question it contains is this : Does your constituency require any public works? If so, would you recommend that it be done by public competition or day labour? Thus inviting the Reform candidates all over Canada to take this circular into the election and tell the voters to say Whether they required a public work, and also whether that work should be put up to public competition or be done by day labour. That circular, signed by a cabinet minister, was sent out to the Reform candidates all over Canada. No doubt many hon. gentlemen behind the Minister of Public Works received that circular.
That was a long time ago.

It was just prior to the election of 1900. I read it at the time in the presence of hon. gentlemen opposite, and not one dared rise in his place and contradict me. Therefore, if there is flagrant partisanship in the Public Works Department-
Which there is not.

It was introduced into the department by this government. Talk about partisanship, why up in Wellington, when the government were selecting a site for a public building,_ an advertisement was put in the papers calling all the Reformers of the village together for the purpose of selecting a sue.
I deny that.
Does the hon. gentleman deny that there appeared in a newspaper in that village-
What newspaper?
I will give the name. Does he deny that there was an advertisement calling the Reformers together in order to decide what site should toe selected for a public building?
I utterly deny that statement. There never was such a thing done in North Wellington.
When the hon. gentleman was in his seat the other day it was stated in answer to that charge: ' Oh, but the government did not select the site which the Reformers named.'
I never said a word about it.
The hon. gentleman is barking up the wrong tree.
No, there is no tree I could bark up in which my hon. iriend would not be found in connection with su6h matters.
What paper do you refer to?
The hon. gentleman knows that this was a case which occurred in Wellington county. Did it happen to be in the county of South Wellington?
I represent the north riding.
Did it happen in the other riding?
I cannot tell you. -
I made the statement the other night and it may be that the public building was in the other riding of Wellington. but the statement is all right.
It is not all right. You connected my name with it as the representative of North Wellington, and I certainly deny it and you ought to apologize.

If I am incorrect as regards the riding my hon. friend represents, I still make the statement that an advertisement such as I have described was published in a newspaper in that county, and that may have been in the south riding.
My hon. friend does not suggest that the Public Works Department had anything to do with any public meeting either in South or North Wellington.
The Public Works Department had to do with the circular to which I referred in the beginning of my remarks.

Not at all-not the slightest thing to do with the circular.
_Mr. BLAIN. Why, the document was signed by the acting Minister of Public Works, who was a member of the government at the time.

The hon. gentleman has just been referring to a public meeting of the Liberal electors in the riding of South Wellington, and I understood him to say that the Public Works Department was responsible for that. The department had nothing to do with it.
I was not saying anything of the kind.
That is what I was referring to.

I was pointing out that at the very root of this partisanship was this circular to which I have alluded and which no minister of the Crown has ever cared to deny.
Seaforth public building, $15,000.

It is expected to cost about $20,000 without the site. The postal revenue is $6,050, customs duties $14,615, money orders issued $25,610, money orders paid $31,359. Nine years ago Seaforth had a population of 2,300.
When was the first vote?
Has the work started?

The plans are being prepared, and the lots have been purchased. We paid to one gentleman $1,300, and to the other $2,700. The two lots cost $4,000. The land is quite large. The frontage is 91 feet, and the depth 132 feet.
In what riding is this?
South Huron. Seaforth is a good town. Its postal revenue is about $6,000. '
Was the old building burned down?

There is no building there now.
M,r. LANCASTER. Who selected this1-site?
An expert of the department.
Did the expert send in a report?	[DOT]
Yes.
Has the minister that report here?
No, not here.
What will be the total cost for this Seaforth building?
It will cost $20,000 exclusive of the land.
What about the fittings? And what will be the total cost of the building ready to occupy?

The chief architect informs me that the fittings will bring the co^t up to something like $25,000-not exceeding that.
Sudbury public building, $20,000.
This is in the constituency of my genial friend from Nipissing (Mr. Gordon). He will agree with me that Sudbury is an important town and well entitled to this public building.
This was in the estimates prior to 1908?
Yes.
Have the plans been prepared?
They are not yet ready.
Is it the intention to commence building this year?
That is the present intention.
The building now in use there is far from being large enough. I hope work on the new building will be started soon.
I assure my hon. friend we. expect to start this year.
When was the estimate for this building first put in?

And the minister states it is the intention to spend the money this year. I presume that the necessary corollary is that there is to be an election next year?
Tilbury public building, $15,000.
The lot for this has been bought. Tilbury and Tilbury east together had a population in 1901 of 4,200.
Is this a new vote, or is it one of the election votes?
Leave out the alternative and I will answer. We calculate to get this building for about $15,000.
In what constituency is it?
In West Kent.

No, in South Essex.
Air. PUGSLEYL However, it is needed in whatever constituency it is. We have a fine lot with 108 feet frontage, and a depth of 99 feet.
What did the site cost?

It cost $1,975.
Tillsonburg public building, $25,000.

Tillsonburg is in South Oxford. The postal revenue last year -was $7,500; customs revenue $25,000; money orders issued $26,000 ; money orders paid' $23,000. Hon. members will see that it is an important place. The population, in 1908, according to Lovell's 'Gazetteer' was 3,000.
What is the building to cost?
It is to cost $25,000 in addition to the site.
Are you renting there now?
Yes.
At what rental?
For the post office, $375 ; for customs house, $160.
When was the first vote?^

Is it the intention of the minister to bring down a supplementary estimate for a public building at Sturgeon Falls. He is aware that two years ago a lot was purchased there for that purpose. And less than a year ago the post office there was burned down. At present, the postal business is being carried on in a building which probably did not cost more than $300. It is simply a 'disgrace to allow the post office to toe carried on any longer in such a building.

I cannot give an assurance that an amount will be put in the estimates this year for the purpose referred to. Of course, that is a matter I cannot speak of until the estimates are brought down. But the outlook for Sturgeon Falls is not sufficiently good just now to warrant us in undertaking the expenditure for a public building.

Does the hon. minister mean the political outlook?
Mr. PUGSLEY". The sulphite mill there has not been running since 1906, and I believe that the mill and the timber limits are now in the courts, and are about being sold, if they have not been sold already. Until prospects improve, we should hardly be justified in the expenditure for such a building as we contemplated at Sturgeon Falls. However, the matter is under consideration, and I cannot say at present what will be done in regard to the estimates of this year.

The mills the Minister of Public Works has referred to will be sold in April, and after that the business will be much larger than it is at present. If something is not put in the estimates now and a building started within a short time, matters will go from bad to worse. Even now it is simply a disgrace to allow any government business to be done in such a building as we have there. The revenue at present is $3,611; postal orders issued, $22,300 last year. In view of the fact that in other places with seven or eight hundred population and a revenue about the same, buildings worth $15,000 or $20,000 are being erected, I think I have a right to complain. Unlike some other members here, I realize that we who are

in opposition cannot expect much in the way of getting public buildings. I would have no complaint to make if these buildings which are being put up in towns represented by supporters of the government were put up in places where the revenue justified the expenditure. But when they are being put up in these little obscure places where there is very little revenue, I think we have some reasonable cause for complaint. In this instance particularly, I think the Postmaster General would be justified in seeing that something was done forthwith. I hope he will take the matter up. Now, I am not asking for any other building in the constituency I represent, although I may mention that so far as the revenue is concerned, we could present strong claims. Take for instance, Cobalt. Last year the revenue was $25,756; postal orders issued, $486,000, Cobalt ranking with many of the lesser cities of the Dominion. Yet the business there is being carried on in a very poor building not at all fit for the business. I believe something should be done immediately to relieve the situation in these two places particularly. I may say that I am prepared to give the Minister of Public Works all due credit for everything that he does.

I am sure the hon. gentleman will feel that I am endeavouring as far as I can to treat the important constituency which he represents with justice. We are spending a good deal of money in that constituency. We are providing a wharf at Haileybury and another at New Liskeard, we are dredging the river and Lake Temiskaming. we are building a dam atLatchford for the purpose of improving navigation, we have provided for the interprovincial bridge over the North Temiskamiifg, and we are providing now for a public building at Sudbury. I regret that I do not see" my way clear to put in an item for a building at Sturgeon Falls. I do not want to discourage my hon. friend, or his constituency, but the naper mill there has not been operated by the receiver, and business has greatly fallen off. The postal revenue there has decreased a igood deal. It is $600 less than it was four years ago, the customs duties are only about one-fourth what they were four years ago. Money orders paid have increased, but money orders issued are $11,000 less than they were four years ago. However, I hope these industries will be started again, and I can assure my hon. friend that the claims of Sturgeon Falls will have my careful consideration.
What about Cobalt ?

The difficulty we found at Cobalt wras to buy a lot. The prices were away up beyond what we thought was
reasonable. I think it has been arranged to rent temporarily suitable accommodation at Cobalt. I hope before long to be able to visit Cobalt, with my hon. friend the Postmaster General, when the matter of a new post office will have our best consideration.
Uxbridge public building, $15,000.
This is a very deserving expenditure. Would the minister inform the House who recommended the purchase of the lot ?

Uxbridge stands in the same category as most of the buildings in the smaller towns. The population in 1901 -was 1,657. The postal revenue is $4,111; money orders issued, $27,068; money orders paid, $17,854. We have purchased a lot, and propse erecting a building to cost $15,000, exclusive of the site and exclusive of armoury accommodation. My hon. friend asks on whose recommendation the site was bought. In the first place, a strong recommendation was made in the shape of a letter from Mr. Grant, the then member of parliament, 'and from Mr. Alexander Graham.
Will the hon. minister read that letter.

This is the substance oi it:	The erection of a public building at
Uxbridge was recommended by G. D. Grant, Esq., and Alexander Graham, Esq., December 31,	1907. Their letter gives
the population of the town, its industries, speaks of it as being the centre of an excellent agricultural country, drawing its trade from a large section, gives the postal revenue, and presents very strong reasons for the erection of a public building. With regard to the site, I sent an expert from the department who recommended the site which was chosen, and which seemed to meet with general approval at the time.
Did any public bodies, such as the council or board of trade, pass resolutions favouring this site?
I have no record of any.
Had there been any communications from -any public bodies to the minister adverse to this site?

Yes, there was one that, according to my information, has met with the favour of my hon. friend. I do not know whether my hon. friend promoted the action of the council or not, but I understand that the action of the council met with the approval of my hon. friend. The O'Neil site recommended by the council after we had made the pur-

chase of the other will cost $1,500 more, it is very uneven, being about 20 feet higher than the street level, and would necessitate heavy excavation and the erection of a retaining wall. The Hutchinson site which we had purchased before getting this resolution from the council only cost $1,200, and is an infinitely better site. It is on the opposite corner of the same street, and only 40 or 50 feet from the present post office, which situation it has occupied for a quarter of a century. It has a frontage of 60 feet against a frontage of 32 feet' for the O'Neil property, and the town council-I hope I have been misinformed when I say that it has been represented that they were prompted by the hon. gentleman-have asked us to pay $2,700, or more than double the amount, for another property that has little more than half the frontage, and which, according to my information, is situated some 20 feet above the level of the street, a very uneven lot, and one which would be absolutely undesirable in so far as the public interest is concerned.
I desire to inform the House and the minister that in so far as I am personally concerned I have not expressed any opinion or indicated any preference with regard to this matter.
I am glad of it.

I was not. instrumental in securing the council's action in passing a resolution in favour of that particular site ; in fact, I very discreetly kept out of the dispute. The O'Neil lot which is recommended by the town council is central. It is one that could have been purchased infinitely cheaper than the price which the minister mentioned. But the chief Liberal worker in Uxbridge went to Mr. O'Neil and told him to keep up a good, stiff price, that the government were going to purchase it, or secure an option, and that no doubt he would secure his price. He stiffened up his price, but the other man sold his lot simply 'because a few Liberals living in the vicinity were supporting that lot which is situated at their end of the town. I understand that the Minister of Public Works has received a resolution from the town council advocating the purchase of the central lot, which would admittedly serve the municipality much more advantageously than the lot at the other end of the town.
By no means admittedly because the lot we bought is right opposite the present post office which is in the central part of the town.

Because the central post office has been situated in one end of the town for a generation is no Mr. PUGSLEY.
reason why the new post office which will last several generations Should be situated in one end of the town. There is no reason why because it has been in an inconvenient place to a great many citizens who go to the post office it should be located in the same end of the town, and still continue to be an inconvenience. The following resolution was sent to the Minister of Public Works :
To the Hon. W'm. Pugsley, M.P.,
Minister of Public Works, Ottawa.
Whereas the government has decided to erect a post office in the town of Uxbridge.
And whereas the government has purchased the Hutchinson site, which is situated in the west end.
And whereas two-thirds of the population of the said town of Uxbridge reside east of the said Hutchinson site.
And whereas the O'Neil site, which is more centrally located, can be purchased at a reasonable price for the erection of a post office.
And whereas the public library and market buildings are situated on opposite corners to the O'Neil site.
Therefore, the municipal council of the corporation of the town of Uxbridge do strongly recommend the honourable Minister of Public Works to purchase the O'Neil site, believing that the _ erection of a post office on the said O'Neil site would be in the interest of the great majority of the residents of the said corporation.	[DOT]
Dated at Uxbridge the 26th day of November, 1910.
(Sgd.) W. R. BEAL,
Mayor.
W. H. CROSBY, Clerk.
I would suggest that the Minister of Public Works should in future communicate with public bodies representing the municipalities and not with his own private supporters in these various towns. I think he would find that it would work far more satisfactorily, would serve the public much better, and that he would secure better advice. It would not be partisan, biased advice, but the advice of the municipality as represented in the municipal council. I would like to ask if it is the purpose of the minister to erect an adjoining armoury in connection with the post office?
It is intended to provide armoury accommodation.
The options were obtained some time in 1908.
This was voted in the session of 1907-8.
Will the minister kindly tell us the reason of the delay? This is 1911. The people are clamouring for the accommodation and it is very badly needed.

There were several reasons, and not the least was the delay

caused by the inquiry which had to be made about the sites in consequence of the action of the council in urging us to secure a different site. That caused a very considerable delay. Then, there was the delay of a year which took place in common with almost all of the other public buildings owing to the decline of the revenues when it had to stand over. Outside of this I do not know that there has been any undue delay, certainly not more than has been caused in connection with many other buildings. I may repeat what I have already said that we have a great many public buildings for which parliament has made appropriations and the chief architect is working upon the plans one after another as his staff is able to follow up the work.
The resolution passed by council is dated November, 1910, so that there was a delay of two years in the erection of this building before the council took action at all.
But the hon. gentleman approved and made representations in parliament in regard to the unsuitability of the site.
I did not object to the site at all; I was simply urging the erection of a building.
My information is that the hon. gentleman made representations with regard to the site as well.
Are the plans prepared?
The plans have been prepared and now are in the Post Office Department for approval.
Will the work be done by contract or day labour?
By public tender and contract. All pulblic buildings are done by public tender and contract.
When may we expect the advertisement to appear?
I cannot tell until we get the plans back from the Post Office Department.
In the course of a jnonth or two?	[DOT]
In the course of a couple of months or so; I cannot tell exactly.
Not longer than two or three months?

I would not like to say because I do not exactly know.
Wallaceburg public building, $15,000.
We want a little information about this.

This is for the purpose of erecting a public building in Wallaceburg. We have purchased a good site at the corner of Nelson and James streets 60 x 90. The postal revenue is $6,603, customs revenue $235,410, money orders issued $18,038, money orders paid $16,124, imports $1,279,308. We propose that this building shall be for post office and customs purposes. We have bought the site for $3,000.
On whose recommendation?
This has been urged by Mr. Gordon.
What constituency?
East Kent. Wallaceburg is a very important and growing town.
What will be the cost of the building complete and ready to occupy?

$20,000 estimated, outside of the land.
Waterloo public building, $41,000.

Waterloo is a very important place. We have a contract already let for the erection of the building. We have bought the land for $5,000; we have let the contract for $36,975, fittings, lock boxes, &c., $5,000; sidewalks, &c-., $1,000; contingencies and superintendence, $2,669; total probable cost, inclusive of the site, heating apparatus, wiring, fittings, furnishing, &c., $51,072.69. The building is for post office, custom house and accommodation of G Company, Waterloo regiment. Postal revenue last year, $11,423; mail orders issued, $17,922; mail orders paid, $66,414. In revenue, $509,941; estimated customs revenue, $60,666. It is in the constituency of Waterloo North.
The constituency of the Minister of Labour.
When were the plans approved by the departments concerned?
Contract entered into on 3rd October. This was voted in 1907 and 1908.
Just before the election. When were the plans approved by the departments concerned?
In June or July.
Is the minister sure of that?
That is what the deputy minister tells me, to the best of his recollection.
Then there is no necessity for waiting longer to let the contract than three or four months after the approval of the plans.
In the ordinary course I would think not.
What would be the extraordinary course that would entail longer delay.

If there were a considerable number of plans approved at the one time the specifications would have to be printed and take their turn at the Printing Bureau, and then the working plans have to be prepared after the approval. How long it will take depends on the quantity of worS on hand; my hon. friend can see that.
I can see that. If that is the outside time required in one constituency it should be the outside time required in another.
Not necessarily.
I suppose the preparing of the specifications is done in order of the approval of the plans.
That does not follow.
Why should you change the order.
The chief architect is allowed to use his .iudgment as to that.
Does the minister think it not dangerous to leave that to the chief architect? Surely the minister is responsible for seeing that justice is done in the several constituencies.
My hon. friend would not expect me to look after these details.
I have a strong suspicion that the minister does look into them carefully. Does he state that _ there is absolutely no interference from himself after the plans are approved.

I would not like to say that, because sometimes if there is a strong complaint made to me as to the delay I may send a memo or telephone the chief architect asking for the cause, and he gives me what I always thought was a reasonable explanation of the delay. To that extent I do interfere. He might think that I thought it desirable to proceed with that particular building and probably he would look into it. I cannot recall any particular case in which it has hurried him up, tout that is what I sometimes do.
So that the member for the constituency can do nothing once the plans are approved.

I remember in the case of the Portage la Prairie building, that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Meighen), wrote me about it, and I sent a memo at once to the chief architect asking what caused the delay, and I was informed the plans had Mr. MEIGHEN.
been sent to the Militia Department for approval. I followed that up in order to see -what was the delay there. I can assure my hon. friend that I gave no instructions which would cause or justify any delay. I made the usual inquiries with regard to the building at Portage la Prairie that I do in respect to those in constituencies represented toy our friends.
Have the working plans and specifications been prepared in that case ?

They have not been fully prepared, but are pretty nearly prepared.
Wiarton public building, $10,000.
Where is Wiarton ?

North Bruce. I had the pleasure of visiting Wiarton last summer and I was very much impressed with the necessity of a public building there. Wiarton is situated upon the lake and they have a little bit of a building, which is totally inadequate for the accommodation of the people. We had a splendid public gathering and I looked at the Mayor's office, which was no better than the post office, and I told him that if he would undertake to erect a new building which would be a credit to the street, I would consider the question of a postoffice.
Did you go any further than that ?
That is all.

Is the minister sure
he spoke to	the mayor,	because	there	isno mayor, reeve.	This is a	village	with	a

Oh,		yes, there is		a
mayor, and a fine looking mayor too.
He is a fine looking man, but he is not a mayor, unless the village became a town last year.

We have not yet purchased the site, but we propose putting up a building at a reasonable cost of perhaps $15,000 or $20,000. Wiarton has an excellent harbour, which is being improved, and it is not only a good town at present, tout it has an excellent future.
Who urged this public building?
Mr. Tolmie.
It would be interesting to know if his worship the mayor has kept his part of the bargain?
I think it is quite certain he would.
There was a sugar refinery there a few years ago that was closed up. That seems to be an objection in the Sturgeon Falls item.
It has not affected this [DOT]town because the revenue here shows an increase.
My hon. friend was up there in the summer and rather suggested he might do something for them.
I was very much impressed with the necessity of doing something.
Is there any correspondence about the site?
Not yet, I thought there would be no difficulty in getting a site at a moderate price.
What is the population? .
Nine years ago it was 2,423.
I thought the minister intended to keep the cost of buildings in such towns below $15,000.
This is larger than usual. I was speaking rather of places under 2,000.
Who is the mayor?
Mr. German, a very excellent man indeed; he is a Conservative.
That is why you were so much impressed by him.
I was impressed, there is no question about that. I think Mr. Tolmie, the hon. member for the constituency was able to point out the advantages of the town.

Is it the minister's intention to put the officers at work on this plan and start this building before other buildings for which votes have been standing for two or three years are commenced?
Mr. PUGSLEYL I have no present intention of doing so.
Is it the rule of the department to have the buildings taken in turn?
Not an inflexible rule.

In fact a very flexible rule. In the county of Ontario there are two votes, one in Whitby, which was taken in the fall of 1908 when the elections were on, and one in my town of Uxbridge. To-day, South Ontario being represented by a Liberal, the Whitby building is completed, but for the Uxbridge
building the working plans have not been commenced. That is not a fair way to treat the members of the House. The minister has put a vote in the estimates this year for a public building in Port Perry. Will he allow the Port Perry building to be erected before the Uxbridge building?
The intention to provide a public building in Port Perry will not prevent the building at Uxbridge going on with reasonable speed.
Will you proceed with the Port Perry building before the Uxbridge building?
I have no present intention of doing so.
Would that not be a great hardship on the Uxbridge people.	.

That would depend on the circumstances.
